headline: Forty Years On: Survivors Recall the June Days
dek: As a memorial to the 1956 riots is unveiled near the old collective-farm market, Iradis and Russians who lived through them remember five days that Soviet histories left out.
paragraphs: Forty years ago this morning, a soldier at a vehicle checkpoint on the road into Talas fired at a cart that had not stopped and killed the horse of an elderly widow on her way to the collective-farm market. By 18 June, after troops had entered the city under martial law, the June days were over. For more than thirty years the Soviet press called them "hooligan disorders" and the official histories of the republic left them out.
Today a bronze statue of a riderless horse will be unveiled near the site of the old market, in keeping with the Fallen Rider tradition,.

Joldoshbek Mamasaliev was eighteen and an apprentice fitter at the railway maintenance yard. On 15 June he marched with the yard's workers to the city soviet building. "We went to ask for the soldier to be tried," he said. "By night it was something else, and I am not proud of all of it." Three weeks later he was arrested. He was one of more than a thousand Iradis detained that summer, and he spent four years in a labor camp.

Nina Gorbunova, whose family lived in one of the new apartment blocks near the boulevard, remembers the other side of those nights. Crowds attacked Russian-owned shops, flats and cars. Her family hid for two days in the home of an Iradi neighbor. "People ask me which side I was on," she said. "I was on the side of the woman who hid us." The internal security files opened after 1992 list 14 dead. Researchers comparing them with church burial registers say the true figure was higher.

headline: Scholars mark 1,250 years since the battle on the Talas
dek: A Talas State University conference and a new memorial stone west of the city recall the summer of 751, when Abbasid and Tang armies met in the valley.
paragraphs: Historians from Talas State University and visiting scholars from Almaty, Tashkent and Bishkek opened a three-day international conference yesterday on the Battle of Talas, fought in the valley in July 751 between the armies of the Abbasid Caliphate and Tang China. The anniversary is the 1,250th of the only recorded battle between the caliphate and China.

On the eve of the conference a memorial stone was set beside the road west of Talas, near the river plains toward Kara-Buura that Iradi historians identify as the battlefield. Speakers at the opening session acknowledged that no battlefield has been found by archaeologists, and that colleagues in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan argue for sites farther down the valley.

The Chinese chronicles describe five days of fighting near the town they called Daluosi, ending when the Karluk troops serving with the Tang army changed sides. Several of the first day’s papers questioned the two claims most often attached to the battle: that it decided whether Central Asia would be Chinese or Muslim, and that Chinese prisoners taken at Talas carried papermaking to Samarkand. “Paper was known in Central Asia long before 751,” said Asylbek Usubaliev, a historian at the university and one of the organizers. “But the story has survived every correction, and we should ask why.”

Other speakers noted that a Christian community was still recorded in Talas in 893, more than a century after the battle, a point that sits uneasily with the school-textbook account of a sudden end to the valley’s Christian past.

headline: Herders Petition Legislature over Kara-Suu Gold License
dek: A delegation of Talas Alatau herders led by the Tanıp elder Bektur Zhumabek uulu asked lawmakers to stop open-pit gold exploration in the upper Kara-Suu valley.
paragraphs: Herders from the Talas Alatau delivered a petition to Legislative Hall yesterday asking the Territorial Legislature to halt an exploration license for open-pit gold mining in the upper Kara-Suu valley. The delegation was led by Bektur Zhumabek uulu, who was acclaimed biy of the Tanıp clan by a clan assembly in 2001 and who has opposed the leasing of communal grazing land to mining companies.

The license covers summer pastures used by Tanıp families, and the herders say the clans were not consulted before it was issued. Their petition asks that the license not be renewed when it expires, and that no open-pit working or cyanide leaching be allowed in the watersheds that feed the Kara-Suu. Small-scale panning for placer gold on the river's gravel bars, which the clans already supervise, would continue.

"Gold can be taken from the river by hand, as our fathers took it. A pit takes the mountain and the water with it," Bektur told reporters through an interpreter. He conducts his business in Iradi. Several herders also cited the Soviet uranium tailings at Mailuu-Suu as a warning of what mining can leave behind in a mountain valley.

A spokesman for the territorial natural resources office said the license had been issued for exploration only, under the territory's mining rules, and that any application to begin mining would require an environmental review and public hearings. Members of the House of Representatives who received the petition said they would ask the office for the license file.

headline: Ten years of Homer's kazy
dek: IradOne will show “The Steppe Family Robinson” again this week. A decade on, the joke turned out to be on the Americans as much as on us.
paragraphs: Ten years ago, when most Iradis knew it only from news reports and copied tapes brought from the air base, this newspaper called the horsemeat scenes in “The Steppe Family Robinson” “a joke at our expense that we will survive.” Church and clan leaders were less forgiving, and in March 1994 the Territorial Legislature passed a resolution regretting the episode’s “mockery of the Iradi people’s customs”.

We survived it. This week, in the week of the Feast of St. Janyl, IradOne will show the episode again, dubbed into Iradi, as it has every August since 1995. Children who were not born when Homer ate eleven sticks of kazy at a border bazaar can recite the High Commissioner’s lecture. And our language has a new expression: Homerdin kazysy, Homer’s kazy, for a foreigner’s well-meant blunder.

Look again and the episode laughs hardest at Iradimania itself: at Krusty’s charity album, at the “cowboys” of the songs who turn out to live in apartment blocks, at Americans who loved a country they had not visited. The settlement that took it off American screens has, since 2001, sent its Iradi license fees to the St. Luka Community Health Mission. Few jokes have paid for as many clinics.
Lisa tells the crowd that she found “a real country” that is “better than the song”. It is a generous line. Ten years on, it is worth asking whether we have been as generous to ourselves.

headline: The Last Provocateur: An Interview with Beknur Karimov
dek: Twenty-one years after he was barred from Soviet studios, the director of Zalmax's Dominion is still making things nobody will broadcast.
paragraphs: Beknur Karimov receives visitors in a studio in Talas cluttered with felt offcuts, carpet fragments and cans of Soviet industrial film bought by the kilogram. At 63 he no longer makes features. He has not made one since Kyz Bulak (Maiden's Spring), the 1982 film that Goskino shelved when he refused to cut its explicit scenes, and that cost him his post at Talasfilm and his right to direct at any Soviet studio. He spent the rest of the 1980s painting and working as a night watchman at a museum in what was then Kobozev.

Since 1992 he has made low-budget video works, splicing found footage of Soviet factories with felt and carpet patterns, and shown them in galleries here and in Almaty. Meanwhile bootleg tapes of his 1977 film Zalmax's Dominion, his Iradi remake of John Boorman's Zardoz, have made him a cult figure among students in Talas and Nurzhan.
IradOne has never broadcast any of his films. Asked why, Karimov smiled. "Their unsuitability for families," he said. "I have always been very consistent about that."

He does not dispute the phrase he used of himself at a meeting of the Talasfilm artistic council in 1981, "pervert of the screen". "They thought it was a confession," he said. "It was a job description."

headline: Amanbek Alimbekov, founder of the Republic, dies at 66
dek: The historian who proclaimed the Republic of Irad in March 1992 and signed the treaty that saved besieged Talas died at his home after a long illness.
paragraphs: Amanbek Alimbekov, the historian who was elected Provisional President on 11 March 1992 and proclaimed the Republic of Irad, died yesterday at his home in Talas after a long illness. He was 66. The territorial government declared a day of mourning.

Born on 9 May 1938 in Iyık Janyl he studied history at Moscow State University and taught at Talas State University from its early years. His research on the revolt of 1916 cost him his department and, by his own account, the right to publish. In 1988 he founded the Ene-Til society, which campaigned for the Latin alphabet and the reopening of churches.

After the Winter Uprising he chaired the council that took over the administration of Talas. He stayed in the city throughout the siege of 1992, and on 2 June, with the water cut and the defenders short of ammunition, he signed the treaty with US Secretary of State James Baker in the basement of the damaged municipal theater. He later wrote that he regarded the loss of independence as the price of saving the city, and that his main condition had been the clause returning sovereignty to the people of Irad if the United States ever ended its administration.

He never joined a party and declined to stand in the territory's first elections, writing that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory. From 1995 he was chancellor of Talas State University. A funeral liturgy will be held at the Church of St. Janyl in Iyık Janyl, where he will be buried. He is survived by his wife and two children.

headline: Talasbank limits cash withdrawals as depositors queue
dek: Long lines form outside branches as savers rush to take out dollars after Washington's withdrawal from the 1992 treaty.
paragraphs: Talasbank yesterday limited cash withdrawals from its branches after a second day of long queues by depositors trying to take out their dollar savings, following the withdrawal of the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty on Sunday.

Under the limits announced by the bank's management, customers may withdraw only a fixed amount of cash each day from dollar and som accounts. Transfers between accounts and card payments are unaffected. Lines formed before dawn outside the bank's head office in the Silk Road Financial Tower and outside branches in Talas and Nurzhan, and several branches closed early after running short of dollar banknotes.

The bank said the limits were temporary and that deposits were safe. "The bank is solvent. What we are short of is paper, not money," a senior manager said. Talasbank, chartered in 1993, holds most commercial deposits in the territory, the escrow accounts for its main exports and many government payrolls.

Bankers in Talas said the immediate question was whether the bank's American correspondent banks, through which it settles dollar payments, would continue to deal with it while the territory's legal status remains unclear. The Supreme Court is considering an emergency petition by Bakyt Orozbekov, the former chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, on whether the territory's statutory independence clause has now taken effect.

headline: Toktarov Proclaims Special Economic Zone from Nurzhan
dek: The former Senate majority leader declares an emergency administration and annuls the Supreme Court's independence ruling; the cabinet in Talas calls the proclamation unlawful.
paragraphs: Erlan Toktarov, the former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, yesterday proclaimed an "Irad Special Economic Zone" from Nurzhan and said it would govern as an emergency administration. Reading a decree at the city administration building on the central square, Toktarov declared the Supreme Court's independence ruling of December annulled and said that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a referendum on unification.

Toktarov said he had taken control of the Democratic Party of Irad. He had warned in December against the immediate proclamation of the Democratic Republic, and he accused the cabinet of selling the country's assets "by auction to its friends". Municipal police lent by the Nurzhan city council, where the Labor Party holds the majority, and gendarmerie units from the Chu lowlands took up positions last night around the city administration, the rail yards and the NurGaz tank farm. Labor councillors said they backed the move to restore order.

In Talas, a spokesman for Prime Minister Bakyt Orozbekov said the cabinet did not recognize the proclamation, which he called "a seizure of power with no basis in law", and that the government of the Democratic Republic remained the lawful authority. The proclamation follows weeks of protest over the cabinet's sale of oil concessions, grain elevators and mobile frequencies, which documents published by the Irad Times link to companies close to ministers and other party members. NurGaz, whose president Kamran Bekzatov has refused to recognize the oil auctions, made no comment last night.

headline: Hospitals full as siege tightens
dek: St. Luka Hospital and the regional hospital are treating wounded civilians and fighters from all sides, with medicines running short and roads into the city cut.
paragraphs: The hospitals of Talas are full. Five weeks after the Popular Front of Irad began its investment of the city on 22 April, doctors at St. Luka Hospital and the Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex said yesterday that they had no free beds and were treating patients in corridors.

St. Luka Hospital, run by the St. Luka Community Health Mission of the Syro-Iradi Church, has 120 beds. Staff said it was caring for well over that number, among them civilians wounded in the fighting on the city's edges, fighters of the Front, men of the National Guard units stationed in the city, and police. "We do not ask anyone which side they are on," said a sister of the Order of St. Janyl the Hermit who works on the surgical ward. "We ask where it hurts."

With the roads to the countryside cut, the hospitals depend on stocks of medicines that staff said would last days rather than weeks. Surgical dressings and anesthetics were the most urgent needs. Power cuts have forced the hospitals to run on generators for several hours each night, and fuel is scarce.

The mission appealed to all sides to allow medical supplies into the city and to respect the hospitals. The cabinet of Prime Minister Bakyt Orozbekov said it was doing everything possible to keep the hospitals supplied. The Front's commanders, who now hold most of the countryside around the city, could not be reached for comment.

headline: Beef plants reopen as roads clear
dek: SuKarne and Conagra resume slaughtering in the western corridor as the ceasefire holds, and families flown out in April begin to return to Semiz.
paragraphs: Cattle trucks were moving again yesterday on the Trans-Talas Highway as the beef plants of the export zone in western Talas resumed operations after months of interruption during the fighting around the city.

SuKarne said it had restarted slaughtering at its complex and expected to return to full shifts within weeks, as feeder cattle began arriving again from the Talas and Chu valleys. The neighboring Conagra plant also reopened. Road links between the western corridor and central Talas, cut for much of the spring and summer, have been open since the ceasefire signed in Bishkek this month.

In Semiz, families are returning. About 1,400 women and children were flown out on Iradiya charters from the aprons beside Talas Air Base after the Popular Front invested the city in April. Most of the men stayed. Through the spring the parish of St. Yusup the Worker sheltered residents, and beef from SuKarne's cold store was handed out in the western corridor when food ran short. Night watches organized by residents kept Semiz free of the looting seen in the city center. Community organizations took no side in the conflict.

Three Semiz residents died during the investment of the city. One of them was a Mexican maintenance engineer at the SuKarne plant. Parishioners said a memorial Mass would be held for all three when the families who left in April have returned.

headline: Memorial to 1937 Deportees Unveiled at Nurzhan Station
dek: Seventy years after Korean families were unloaded from freight cars at Kobozev, their descendants and the Iradis who helped them gathered by the rail yards.
paragraphs: Several hundred people gathered yesterday beside the freight yards of Nurzhan station for the unveiling of a memorial to the Koreans deported from the Soviet Far East in 1937, seventy years after the first trains arrived.

In the autumn of 1937 several thousand deportees were unloaded from unheated freight cars here, at what was then Kobozev, and at sidings along the Chu valley. Many spent their first winter in dugouts in the steppe. The memorial, a granite block bearing inscriptions in Korean, Russian and Iradi, was paid for by subscription through the Korean cultural association founded in the city in 1990. It stands at the edge of the yards where, according to the association, the first trains were unloaded.

Speakers returned again and again to the help that Iradi villagers and church communities gave the deportees, sharing food and shelter through that first winter. "My grandmother said that the first bread she ate in this country was given to her by a woman who had very little herself," one association member told the crowd. Catholic and Presbyterian clergy blessed the memorial together, and elderly residents laid flowers.
The association said that commemorations would be held at the memorial each autumn.

headline: Former prime minister charged in absentia
dek: Prosecutors accuse Bakyt Orozbekov, who has lived in Istanbul since last year, of abuse of office over the privatization auctions of early 2007.
paragraphs: ISEZ prosecutors yesterday charged Bakyt Orozbekov, the only Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of Irad, in absentia with abuse of office in connection with the sale of state assets by his cabinet in January and February 2007.

The charge sheet, filed with the Talas District Court, concerns the auctions of oil and antimony exploration concessions, state grain elevators and blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum, and the cabinet's decree privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. A spokesman for the Attorney General said the office would ask the Turkish authorities for Mr. Orozbekov's return. He declined to say whether former ministers would also be charged.

Mr. Orozbekov, 45, was arrested at his official residence when the Popular Front stormed Talas on 4 June last year, signed an instrument of resignation and was handed over to a United Nations compound outside the city. He left Irad later in the year under arrangements made by UN officials and now lives in Istanbul. In a statement issued there through his office, he called the charges political and repeated that the auctions had been open. He has previously denied any personal involvement in the transactions that were later criticized.
The court has not set a date for a hearing. Mr. Orozbekov's lawyers in Talas said they had not yet received the charge sheet.

headline: Kemel Ishakov, the voice of the passes, dies at 78
dek: The author of Akyrky Ashuu, who wrote the flight of 1916 into Soviet literature and later asked both sides to spare Talas, has died.
paragraphs: Kemel Ishakov, Irad’s national novelist, whose Akyrky Ashuu (The Last Pass) carried the story of the 1916 flight across the Soviet Union and into more than twenty languages, died in Talas yesterday. He was 78.

He was born Kemel Ishak uulu on 9 October 1930 in Arsha-Say, below the Talas Alatau, to a Christian family of horse herders on the local collective farm. His grandmother had survived the flight to Xinjiang in 1916. His father, Ishak, was jailed for eight years after the wartime mobilization strike of 1944 and came home in 1953. Kemel graduated in Iradi and Russian philology from the Talas Pedagogical Institute in 1952, taught at the village school and wrote for Iradyn Chyny.

Kök Jal (Grey Mane, 1959), the story of an old herder hiding a grey stallion through a winter, was read by every Iradi as a book about 1944 though it never said so. Akyrky Ashuu followed in 1964 and won the State Prize of the Iradi SSR in 1966; the censors cut its last chapter, with its rider in white on the pass, which was restored in 1990. His novel Ünsüz Koñguroo (The Silent Bell) waited until 1989 to appear in full in Iradi.

He chaired the Union of Writers from 1986 to 1991, received the first Altyn-Zhylky lifetime award in 1996, and in March 2007 signed the open letter asking both sides to spare Talas. He was buried in Arsha-Say.

headline: Kamran Bekzatov at Sixty
dek: The NurGaz president, born in Kobozev two years after the 1949 oil strike, turns sixty today.
paragraphs: Kamran Bekzatov was born in Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, on 28 January 1951, two years after oil was struck in the lower Chu basin. His father, Rashid Bekzatov, was chief engineer at the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant, and his mother, Valentina Bekzatova, was a physician at the city polyclinic. He went to Russian-language schools, and in 1969 he left for Moscow to study at the Gubkin Institute of the Petrochemical and Gas Industry, graduating in 1974 as a petroleum reservoir engineer.

For the next fourteen years he worked in the oilfields of Western Siberia under the USSR Ministry of the Oil Industry, rising from field engineer to chief engineer of a production unit near Nizhnevartovsk. In 1988 he came home as general director of Iradneft, the republic's oil production trust, and brought with him the water-injection methods and rotary drilling equipment that slowed the decline of the aging Chu fields.

In 1993 Iradneft became NurGaz, and Bekzatov has led the company since. Its Northern Export Feeder, opened in 2000, carries crude to the Kazakh network near Shymkent, and NurGaz is now the largest commercial taxpayer in the zone. He has never stood for office. A company spokeswoman said he would mark the day privately with his wife, Galina, and their three children.

headline: Tribal Delegates Walk Out of Unification Talks
dek: The Iradi Freedom Society delegation left the UN-supported talks after the DPI offered the tribal regions one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.
paragraphs: The delegation of the Iradi Freedom Society walked out of unification talks at the headquarters of the UN mission here yesterday, after the Democratic Party of Irad offered the tribal regions one-third of the seats in a unified Territorial Legislature. The talks were the first direct negotiations between the two sides since the Bishkek ceasefire of 2007 and grew out of the referendum initiative proposed in 2008.

According to IAC delegates, the DPI proposals also sought state control over the mountain water catchments. Bektur Zhumabek uulu, who led the delegation, said the offer reflected neither the tribal regions' two-thirds share of the territory nor their share of the population. "The mountains were given by God to the horses and the herds, not to the stock exchanges of Talas," he said as the delegates left the hall. The Karakoyun elder Biybolot Moldosh uulu was among those who walked out with him.

A DPI spokesman said the party's proposals "remain on the table" and that seats had been apportioned according to official population figures. Other questions, including whether the El-Choro riders would be merged with the State Defense Corps, were left unresolved. UN officials said the mission remained available to both sides. No date has been set for further talks.

headline: Four miners killed in Sary-Bulak rockfall
dek: The men were working on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 at the Sary-Bulak Antimony Works when the roof collapsed.
paragraphs: Four miners were killed on Tuesday night when a rockfall brought down part of a working on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 at the Sary-Bulak Antimony Works, the company said yesterday.

Rescue teams recovered the bodies of the four men yesterday morning, after clearing fallen rock through the night. Two other miners on the same shift were brought to the surface with minor injuries and treated at the polyclinic in the workers' settlement. The company said the names of the dead would not be released until all their families had been informed.

Production in Shaft No. 2, the "Severny" shaft sunk in the 1970s, has been halted while state mining inspectors examine the site. Work continues in Shaft No. 1 and in the Central incline. A company spokesman said it was too early to say what had caused the fall, and that the works would "cooperate fully with the inspectorate".

The works, the largest employer in Sary-Bulak District with about 2,300 staff, are the mining arm of the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine. In the settlement beside the mine, known locally as Rudnik, residents gathered outside the mine office yesterday as news of the deaths spread. A memorial service will be held at the settlement's Syro-Iradi parish church.

headline: Vasily Chernov, last leader of the Socialist Republic, dies in Moscow
dek: The refinery engineer who led the Communist Party of Irad from 1986 and proclaimed the Socialist Republic in 1991 had lived in Russia since the surrender of August 1992.
paragraphs: Vasily Chernov, the last First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad and the only President of the Socialist Republic of Irad, died in Moscow on Wednesday. He was 76. His family said he would be buried at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery. The ISEZ government has made no official comment.

Born in Kobozev, now Nurzhan, on 14 March 1935, the son of a railway locomotive mechanic, Chernov trained as a chemical engineer in Leningrad and spent sixteen years at the city's refinery, rising to chief engineer before moving into party work in 1974. He became First Secretary in November 1986 and, on 9 October 1991, declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with himself as President.

His government's emergency decrees of November 1991 and the economic collapse that followed provoked the Winter Uprising. On 3 February 1992 riot police opened fire on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002 but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition, and in his memoir he denied giving such an order. From 10 April his forces besieged Talas until the siege was broken in June after the American intervention. After the surrender of 18 August 1992 he was given safe conduct to Russia. In 1995 the territorial attorney general requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his citizenship, and the case never came to trial.

In Nurzhan, where many residents worked for the SRI state, some older people remember him as a capable industrial manager. A group of former SRI officials said they would hold a memorial gathering in the city.

headline: Profile: The Governor's Eldest Son Takes Command of the Gendarmerie
dek: Ruslan Toktarov, 33, trained as a tank engineer in Omsk and oversaw the building of the Qara-Chik checkpoints; he now commands a force of about 4,000.
paragraphs: Major General Ruslan Toktarov, appointed this week by his father to command the Republican Gendarmerie, was born in Talas on 22 June 1978, the first child of Erlan Toktarov, then a junior officer in the Soviet logistics corps, and his wife Anara. His father's postings, including two tours in Afghanistan, kept the boy mostly with his mother in Talas. The family settled in Kobozev in 1989 and returned to Talas after 1992, and Ruslan finished secondary school there in 1995.

Most children of the territorial elite went on to universities in the United States or Western Europe. Ruslan instead enrolled at the Omsk Higher Tank Engineering School in Russia and graduated in 1999 as an armored-vehicle engineer. He later took counter-narcotics and protective-security courses run by American private contractors at Talas Air Base.

After managing security for the family's fuel-distribution business near the base, he joined the Gendarmerie as a captain in 2004. In the spring of 2007 he commanded a detachment guarding the NurGaz tank farm and rail yards outside Nurzhan, and that summer his units were among the DPI forces that entered Talas. As deputy commander of the Border Demarcation Brigade he oversaw the building of the fortified crossings on the Qara-Chik line. Opposition figures attribute his promotion to his family; a Gendarmerie spokesman pointed to his service record.
He is married to Aiperi Toktarova (née Abdyldaeva), and they have three children. A member of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, he plays ulak tartysh for a Gendarmerie team.

headline: Governor's Family Takes Up Residence at Boz-Korgon
dek: Property filings show that the Toktarov family has formally occupied a residential estate inside the former territorial continuity compound east of Nurzhan since last year.
paragraphs: Members of Governor Erlan Toktarov's family have formally occupied a residential estate inside the Boz-Korgon compound, 40 km east of Nurzhan, since 2011, according to property filings in the Chu District land register examined by the Herald. The filings record the estate as a residence within the compound and list permits issued this year for further residential and service buildings.

Boz-Korgon was begun in 1995 by the territorial administration as a continuity-of-government site, with a hardened command and communications center and a security depot for the Nurzhan oil fields and the eastern rail corridor. Underground shelters and a perimeter wall were added between 2001 and 2005, financed through territorial infrastructure bonds, and the site passed to the ISEZ government after 2007.

A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the residence was "a security arrangement appropriate to the office of Governor" and that the compound remained state property. He declined to say how often the Governor stays there. The compound has long been the subject of rumor. In the 2000s tabloids in Talas and Nurzhan claimed that it had been built as a private retreat for the Bush family; territorial records show that construction began more than a decade before the United States withdrew from the treaty, and no document transferring title to anyone has been found.

headline: Twenty years of Swift Hooves
dek: The 1993 American compilation that sang of Irad's "Christian cowboys" still pays for clinics in the mountains, and still divides listeners at home.
paragraphs: Twenty years ago this spring, Swift Hooves went on sale in the United States: a compilation of country and folk songs about Irad, recorded by American artists, with its profits pledged to Christian charities in the new territory. It was the high point of what Americans then called Iradimania, when newspapers and television presented Iradis as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys".

The money outlasted the fashion. The Eparchy of Talas founded the St. Luka Community Health Mission in 1994 partly with proceeds from the album, and the mission's mobile teams began visiting the summer pastures two years later. Since 2001 the mission has also received the fees IradOne pays to show "The Steppe Family Robinson", the Simpsons episode whose parody of the record led to its withdrawal from American screens in 1995.

At home the album's legacy is more mixed. Musicians credit its songs, together with the cassettes smuggled into Soviet Irad in the 1980s, with shaping Iradi country-folk, and "Ride for Talas" is still requested at weddings. Others hear in it an American picture of Irad, painted from Chicago and Nashville, that had little room for the country's Russian-speaking cities or for the herders of the high valleys.

headline: Council Questions Avenue Land Transfers
dek: Opposition members of the Talas city council asked why municipal plots on the central avenue went to companies of the Governor's sons without auction; the municipality says the transfers were lawful.
paragraphs: Opposition members of the Talas city council yesterday questioned the transfer of municipal land along the city's central avenue to companies owned by Alikhan Toktarov and Adil Toktarov, sons of Governor Erlan Toktarov, and asked why the plots had not been offered at competitive auction.

Records presented at the council session show that since 2011 plots on the avenue have been allocated to Alikhan Toktarov's Steppe Luxury Group, to Adil Toktarov's Talas Commercial Development Group and to joint ventures of the two companies, which are building office towers, hotels and leisure venues aimed at foreign contractors and energy executives. Councillors also asked whether the projects had received tax holidays and priority connections from the Talas Municipal Water Authority, and requested the valuations on which the transfers were based.

A deputy mayor told the session that all the transfers were lawful, had been approved under the municipal land regulations and were recorded in the city's published register. He said the council's budget committee could inspect the files. Neither company had responded to the Herald's questions by last night. The council's DPI majority voted against a motion to suspend further allocations on the avenue until the files had been reviewed.

headline: Court Declines Term-Limits Challenge
dek: The Supreme Court says that last year's amendment removing the two-term limit on governors is a matter for the legislature.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court yesterday declined to hear a challenge to last year's amendment to the Elective Governor Acts that removed the limit of two consecutive terms for a Governor, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.

The petitioners, a group of lawyers and voters from Talas, argued that the 1992 Acts form part of the basic law of the ISEZ and that the limit could not be lifted by an ordinary vote that benefited the sitting Governor. Under the prevailing reading of the Acts, Governor Erlan Toktarov's tenure from 2007 to 2011 counted as his first term, and he would have been barred from standing in 2015. The amendment passed in June 2013 by 53 votes to 4, with three abstentions; the Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan voted against it.

In a short order, the five-member court said that the length and number of gubernatorial terms were matters for the Territorial Legislature and that it would not substitute its judgment for that of the chamber. A lawyer for the petitioners said they had no further remedy in the ISEZ courts. A DPI spokesman welcomed the decision as "respect for the separation of powers". The Governor has not said whether he will stand next year.

headline: Council Members Query Water Works Tenders
dek: Opposition councillors asked why some contracts for rebuilding the Talas water treatment works were awarded without open tender.
paragraphs: Opposition members of the Talas city council yesterday questioned the award of some construction contracts for the reconstruction of the Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works without open tender, and asked the municipality to publish the contract files.

The reconstruction, together with the replacement of Soviet-era water mains, is financed with concessional loans and directed by Aidar Maksat, Director-General of Infrastructure Development for the municipality since 2009. Maksat is married to Zara Toktarova, the Governor's daughter. Municipal figures show that losses from the distribution network have fallen markedly since the program began, and councillors on both sides of the chamber praised the improvement in supply to the outer districts.

The questions concerned contracts for pumping stations and sections of trunk main awarded by direct negotiation. Maksat told the session that the contracts had been placed under the emergency provisions of the municipal procurement rules, because the mains concerned were failing, and that each award had been approved by the city's legal department. He offered to give the council's budget committee the full files. The committee chairman said the files would be reviewed at its next meeting.

headline: Derby Abandoned after Riot at NurGaz Stadium
dek: The Kara-Ak derby was stopped in the 62nd minute after fighting between Neftchi and Tulpar supporters spread onto the pitch. About 60 people were hurt and 140 detained.
paragraphs: Sunday’s derby between Neftchi Nurzhan and Tulpar Talas was abandoned in the 62nd minute after fighting between rival supporters spread from the stands onto the pitch at the NurGaz Stadium. About 60 people were injured and the Republican Gendarmerie detained about 140, according to the city health department and a Gendarmerie spokesman.

The trouble began before kickoff, two days after the Victory Day parade in Nurzhan. Neftchi supporters in the east stand, where the Vyshka group gathers, displayed St. George ribbons and a banner reading “Kobozev – Russian city”. Tulpar supporters in the away section replied with the Soviet-era slogan “Suitcase, station, Russia”. Objects were thrown during the first half, and early in the second fans from both ends forced their way onto the pitch. The referee led the players off and the match was not resumed.

Neftchi’s president, Rustam Bekzatov, condemned the violence and said the club would cooperate with the Football Federation of Irad. Tulpar’s owners, the Talas Commercial Development Group, called for “exemplary penalties”.
The federation’s disciplinary committee will meet this week. Officials said away supporters could be banned from future derbies.

headline: Talas and the Clans Protest UNESCO Listing of Kok-Tash
dek: In a rare point of agreement, both the ISEZ government and the tribal elders object that the Silk Roads nomination treats the ancient karez system as Kazakh and Kyrgyz territory.
paragraphs: The Kok-Tash Kariz, the network of underground irrigation channels beneath the foothills of the Talas Alatau, has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as a component of the Silk Roads serial property nominated by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. The Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed was included in the same way. Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention.

The ISEZ government and the Iradi Freedom Society both protested that the nomination treated the sites as Kazakh and Kyrgyz territory. The Department of Public Information said the government had conveyed its objection through the UN mission. Clan elders of the IAC set out theirs in a letter, carried to Kara-Oi by courier, saying that the galleries had been dug and kept by the people of the valleys and that no foreign state had asked their leave.

The system has about 140 km of tunnels, expanded under the Kara-Khanids, and still supplies water to more than 40 villages. Most of it lies on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line, where it is maintained by village councils of elders and water masters. Hydrologists at Talas State University welcomed the international attention but warned that falling groundwater and collapsing galleries threaten its condition.

headline: Supreme Court Upholds Herders' Right of Passage
dek: In a rare recognition of customary practice, the court ruled that herders on their seasonal migrations may drive livestock across industrial highway easements without paying municipal licensing penalties.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court yesterday recognized the customary right of transhumant herders to drive their livestock across industrial highway easements without paying municipal licensing penalties, in a decision that lawyers described as one of the few in which the court has given effect to customary practice.

The case, known in the court list as the Pastoral Transit Case, arose from penalties imposed on herding families who drove sheep and cattle across a highway easement on their spring move from winter quarters to the summer pastures. The municipal authorities had treated the crossings as unlicensed use of the easement and fined the herders for each crossing.

The court held that the herders' right of passage along their migration routes was established long before the easements were created and had not been extinguished by them. It ordered the penalties annulled. Herders' representatives said the decision would ease the spring and autumn migrations, when flocks must cross the main road and rail corridors of the valleys. A lawyer for the municipality said it would study the judgment and review its licensing rules.

headline: Alikhan Toktarov named chairman of IradOne
dek: The Governor has appointed his second son to chair the board of the state broadcaster.
paragraphs: Governor Erlan Toktarov yesterday appointed his son Alikhan Toktarov, 34, chairman of the executive board of IradOne, the state broadcaster, according to a decree published by the Department of Public Information.

Alikhan Toktarov, the Governor's second son, heads the Steppe Luxury Group, which holds regional import rights for European cars, Swiss watches and American electronics and has developed office and hotel projects on the central avenue of Talas. He studied business in Bishkek and media and management at Regent's College in London. He has not previously held a post in broadcasting.

IradOne was created as a public corporation under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1993. Its board is appointed by the Governor, and since 2007 the corporation has been supervised by the Department of Public Information. It launched the Russian-language channel IradOdin in 2009 and began this year to move from analog to digital terrestrial transmission. A DPI spokesman said the new chairman had been chosen for his commercial experience and would lead the broadcaster's modernization. Opposition commentators said the appointment placed the main broadcaster in the hands of the Governor's family. The new chairman made no public statement yesterday.

headline: Profile: IradOne's New Chairman
dek: Alikhan Toktarov, who takes over the state broadcaster at 34, built his career in luxury imports and property.
paragraphs: Alikhan Toktarov, appointed this week to chair the board of IradOne, was born in Talas on 14 September 1980, the second child of Erlan Toktarov and his wife Anara. He grew up mainly in Talas and, from 1989, in Kobozev, and was eleven when the civil war of 1992 began. Under the territorial administration he attended an English-language preparatory school in Talas.

He studied international business in Bishkek from 1998 to 2000 and then moved to London, where in 2003 he took a bachelor's degree in media and management at Regent's College. That year he came home to work in his father's bonded-warehousing business near Talas Air Base. In 2008 he founded the Steppe Luxury Group, which obtained exclusive regional import rights for European cars, Swiss watches and American consumer electronics, and from 2011 he acquired land along the central avenue of Talas for office towers, hotels and leisure venues, several of them joint ventures with his younger brother Adil.

In 2010 he married Madina Toktarova (née Iskakova), a former IradOne presenter; they have two children. He owns racehorses and collects classic cars. He rarely gives interviews, and he has not said what changes he plans at the broadcaster. Colleagues in the property business describe him as a promoter of consumer brands and entertainment, which he has called the future of the Talas economy.

headline: Election Commission Strikes Rival Candidates from Gubernatorial Ballot
dek: The Territorial Election Commission disqualified a union-backed independent and a Russo-aligned businessman under the new signature and residence rules.
paragraphs: The Territorial Election Commission yesterday struck the main rival nominees from the ballot for next month's gubernatorial election, among them Pavel Gritsenko, an independent backed by trade unions in Nurzhan, and Arkady Melnikov, a Nurzhan businessman aligned with the Russo deputies in the legislature.

The commission applied rules adopted by the DPI majority this year, which require a candidate for Governor to submit 10,000 verified signatures of registered voters and to have lived in the ISEZ continuously for ten years before nomination. It said Gritsenko's nomination had fallen short of the verified signatures required after checks against the voter registers, and that Melnikov had not met the residence requirement. A commission member said the rules applied equally to all candidates.

Gritsenko's campaign said the disqualifications were "an election decided in advance" and that it would appeal. Opposition groups announced protests in Talas and Nurzhan. The election on 3 November is the first since the 2013 amendment removed the limit on gubernatorial terms. Governor Erlan Toktarov and Lieutenant Governor Daniyar Tologonov are standing again on the DPI ticket. The DPI said it welcomed "a lawful and orderly campaign".

headline: Suspended sentences for students over banned party leaflets
dek: Three young people convicted under the Extremist Activity Act of handing out Jer-Suu leaflets will not go to prison, the Talas District Court ruled.
paragraphs: The Talas District Court yesterday gave suspended prison sentences to three students convicted of distributing leaflets of the Jer-Suu Party, the nationalist party banned in 2008.

Prosecutors from the Attorney General’s office told the court that the three, aged between 19 and 21, had handed out several hundred leaflets near bus stops and university buildings in the city last autumn. The leaflets reproduced verses by the party’s exiled co-founder Tilek Sharshenov and called for the protection of pastures and water against mining leases. The prosecution had asked for custodial terms. The judge said she had taken into account the defendants’ ages and the absence of any call to violence. The Herald is not naming the students at the request of their families.

Jer-Suu held between two and four seats in the territorial House from 1996 to 2006. In April 2008 the Supreme Court banned it under the Extremist Activity Act, on an application from the Ministry of Internal Security, holding that it had taken part in armed rebellion in 2007. The OSCE and Human Rights Watch criticized the ruling as collective punishment of a lawful party. The party’s writings remain banned.
Defence lawyers said they had not decided whether to appeal.

headline: Sixty years on, Mailuu-Suu still waits
dek: Nearly six decades after a tailings dam broke above the town, the radioactive legacy of Soviet uranium mining is stabilized but not removed, and the money for the next stage has not come.
paragraphs: The river that gives Mailuu-Suu its name, “oily water”, runs past some two dozen dumps of radioactive tailings and as many heaps of waste rock, left in a narrow, landslide-prone valley when the Soviet atomic program stopped mining uranium here in 1968. In 1958 one of the tailings dams failed after heavy rain and sent contaminated material downstream; the accident was never acknowledged in the Soviet period.

International assessments put the volume of tailings in the valley at about 2 million cubic meters. A World Bank-financed project begun under the territorial administration in 2004 stabilized several impoundments, built drainage works and moved the most exposed dump. The war of 2007 halted it, leaving the town on the tribal side of the line; work resumed in 2009 under an arrangement brokered by the UN mission, with contractors and ISEZ engineers admitted by the clan council under UN escort, and was completed in 2012.

Since then the dumps have been watched rather than removed. A warden service of the clan council takes readings with equipment supplied through UNMI, and the geography faculty of Talas State University keeps landslide survey points in the valley. “We measure, we send the numbers, and we wait,” said Bakai Joldoshev, one of the wardens.
Donors have discussed further remediation, but the line and the lack of a recognized government have so far kept the money away.

headline: Tax inspectors fine Herald Publishing over payroll filings
dek: An audit of the company that publishes this newspaper ended with a fine for errors in payroll reporting, which the company has paid.
paragraphs: The ISEZ tax service has fined the Herald Publishing Company, which publishes the Talas Herald, for errors in its payroll reporting, at the end of an audit that began this spring.

The company said it had paid the fine and corrected the filings. In a statement, the editor, Elmira Beishenova, said the paper did not dispute the inspectors’ arithmetic but regarded the inspection as selective. “We are not aware of a similar audit of any other newspaper this year,” she said. The tax service said audits were assigned according to its normal procedures.

The audit followed the withdrawal of advertising from the paper by several state-owned and state-licensed companies after the Herald reported the removal of rival candidates from last year’s gubernatorial ballot. The paper estimates that it has lost about a third of its advertising revenue. The companies have said their decisions were commercial.

Last year the Talas District Court found for the Talas Commercial Development Group on one point of its libel suit over the paper’s 2013 reports on land transfers, ordering a correction and damages of 200,000 som and dismissing the rest of the claim.

headline: Night flood on the Muz-Suu sweeps away bridge; no casualties
dek: A glacial lake at the head of the valley partly burst on Friday night. A radio warning from herders gave the village three hours.
paragraphs: A flood from a glacial lake at the head of the Muz-Suu washed out a road bridge and one of the river’s two canal intakes on Friday night and damaged 14 houses in Tash-Bulak, in Talas District. No one was killed or injured.

The moraine dam of Muz-Köl, a small lake at about 3,300 meters on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line, partly failed late on Friday, according to the Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service. Herders camped below the lake raised the alarm by radio, and the warning reached the village about three hours before the water.

“We heard it before we saw it,” said Gulsara Sarieva, whose kitchen and yard were filled with mud and stones. Families moved to higher ground with their animals, and district police closed the valley road.

By Saturday morning gravel covered about 40 hectares of fields along the river. The district administration said water to farms served by the destroyed intake would be cut until a temporary channel could be dug. The hydrological service said it would ask the clan council on the upper river for access to inspect the lake.

headline: Twenty years of the Golden Horse
dek: The Altyn-Zhylky Awards, born in the territorial years with a lifetime prize for Kemel Ishakov, reach their twentieth ceremony.
paragraphs: When the first Altyn-Zhylky Awards were handed out in Talas in December 1996, the lifetime award went to the novelist Kemel Ishakov, whose Akyrky Ashuu had been read across the Soviet Union and had just appeared in English. Twenty years later the gilded bronze statuette of a galloping horse is the best-known prize in Iradi culture, and next week’s ceremony will be broadcast on IradOne.

The awards were founded during the territorial period to honor film, music and literature, and they have grown with the country’s culture. The categories now include feature and documentary film; popular music, with separate awards for Mor-Wave and its offshoots; and fiction and poetry in Iradi, English and Russian. A separate award goes each year to an artist from elsewhere in Central Asia.

Since 2010 the literary awards have included the Kemel Ishakov Prize for a first book in Iradi, which organizers say has drawn more entries every year as young writers turn from Russian and English to Iradi.

Not everyone is pleased. Some film-makers complain that the film categories reward work that has passed the screening-permit system, and Mor-Wave musicians have long grumbled that the popular music prizes favor acts with television contracts.

headline: Gravestones from Shar-i-Kuhna Surface at Foreign Auctions
dek: Archaeologists say at least three inscribed Christian grave markers offered for sale abroad were taken from the medieval cemetery outside the holy city.
paragraphs: At least three medieval Christian gravestones offered for sale by foreign auction houses in the past year were removed from the cemetery of Shar-i-Kuhna, the ruins of Old Iyık Janyl, archaeologists at Talas State University said yesterday.

The stones are river boulders (kayrak) carved with crosses rising from lotuses and short inscriptions in Syriac and Old Turkic, of the kind recorded by the hundreds in the cemetery east of the town walls. Most of those stones date from between 1240 and 1338. University archaeologists who have worked at the site since 2007 said they had matched two of the stones in the catalogues with photographs in their own survey records. A third bears a personal name recorded in a Soviet-era field notebook.

"These are not loose finds. They were dug out of graves," one of the archaeologists said. Staff at the site have found fresh pits in the eastern part of the cemetery on several occasions in recent years. The ruins, protected as a National Historical Monument, were inscribed with the Church of St. Janyl on the World Heritage List in 2004, but site staff say the cemetery is not guarded outside the pilgrimage season.

Officials in Iyık Janyl said they had informed the Attorney General's office. They acknowledged that Irad's unresolved status, and the fact that it has not been a State Party to the World Heritage Convention since 2006, would make it difficult to press claims for the stones' return. The archeparchy called the removal of the gravestones "a theft from the dead".

headline: Legislature passes bride abduction law
dek: Abducting a woman for marriage will carry five to ten years in prison under an act passed by the legislature yesterday.
paragraphs: The Territorial Legislature yesterday passed the Abduction for Marriage Act, making the abduction of a woman to force her into marriage a specific criminal offense punishable by five to ten years in prison, and by up to twelve where the victim is under 18.

The act also bars registry offices from registering a marriage that began with an abduction. Until now such cases have been prosecuted under general kidnapping provisions and have usually ended in a fine.

Supporters of the bill pointed to the case of Saikal Imanaly kyzy, who was 19 when she was abducted in a Kara-Buura village in 2015 and escaped two days later. Represented by Gulnara Sadykova of the Legal Defense Guild, she pressed charges; the court at Kyzyl-Adyr fined her abductor. The verdict set off the Ak Jooluk, or “white headscarf”, campaign by women’s groups, whose members watched yesterday’s vote from the gallery. Sadykova called the act “a beginning”, adding that its value would depend on prosecutors.

The Syro-Iradi Synod’s 2014 pastoral letter On the Free Consent of Spouses calls bride kidnapping “a sin against the sacrament and against the dignity of women”. The act does not apply in the tribal regions, where clan councils differ on whether an abducted woman who stays is married.

headline: Why Talas tortillas are yellow
dek: Semiz tortillerías could not find white maize when they opened. They found Khrushchev’s instead.
paragraphs: Visitors from Mexico notice it at once: the tortillas sold in Semiz are yellow. Not pale or golden, but the deep yellow of the maize that has grown in the Talas valley since the 1950s.

When the first tortillería opened in Semiz in 2000, its owners looked for the white maize used for tortillas at home and could not find any. What the valley grows is yellow dent field maize, planted since Nikita Khrushchev’s maize drive of 1955 to feed the cattle of the Virgin Lands sovkhozes. A breeding station opened near Kara-Bulak in 1956, and by 1960 maize covered more of the new land than wheat. Today most of the crop is milled for compound feed and fed in the export feedlots west of the city, a few minutes’ walk from the tortillerías.

“We bought feed corn from a farmer and nixtamalized it in a bathtub,” said Rosario Beltrán, whose family runs one of the dozen or so tortillerías now in the district. “It tasted like home, only yellow. After a year nobody wanted white.”

The color has stuck. “Talas tortillas” are sold in the Saturday market alongside jügörü, the boiled maize cobs sold on every street corner in summer, and beef tacos from the export plants have become a staple of student life in the city.

headline: Twenty years on, farmers count the cost of the export zone
dek: The agribusiness zone brought jobs and exports to western Talas. Members of the collective farms whose land it took, and the grain growers who compete with its imports, tell a different story.
paragraphs: Twenty years after the Talas Agribusiness Accord, the export zone on the western edge of the city is one of the territory's great success stories, at least by the measures its administration prefers. Its tenants, led by the SuKarne and Conagra beef plants, ship processed food by rail through Kazakhstan, and thousands of people work inside its fences.

About 220 hectares of the zone's land came from two former collective farms between the city and the airfield that became Talas Air Base. Some of their members say they never received a fair price. Compensation was paid partly in som, and several former members told the Herald that it bought far less than the land was worth. "They told us we were making way for the future," said Mukhtar Usenbaev, 71, who worked as a tractor driver on one of the farms. "The future was very cheap."

Grain farmers in the Talas valley have a newer complaint. Livestock, feed and packaging enter the zone duty-free, and farmers' associations say that tenants' imports of feed grain undercut local growers. The zone administration replies that local suppliers still provide most of the forage for the feedlots, and points to the alfalfa and fodder maize grown for them across the valley.

The zone's roads, rail sidings and power lines were paid for with territorial bonds. Its customs and tax regime was confirmed by the emergency decrees of 2007, and its administration, under the Ministry of Economy, says it is now looking for new tenants.

headline: In Semiz, Spanish with an Iradi Accent
dek: Grandfathers are ata, the bus is a marshrutka and money is counted in som: two decades on, the Spanish of la Colonia has picked up the words of its neighbors.
paragraphs: In the courtyards of la Colonia, children call their grandfathers ata. Their parents pay in som at the Saturday market, ask the aksakal of the stairwell for permission, and take the marshrutka to the bazar. The Spanish of Semiz, brought from Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora twenty years ago, has taken in the words of the city around it.
The borrowing runs both ways. Iradi workers at the beef plants call their foremen jefe, tortilla needs no translation in Talas, and the city’s young people greet their friends as compa.

Most of the second generation is trilingual. Children with Mexican parents attend ISEZ schools, which teach in Iradi and English under the 1997 Language and Education Reform Act, speak Spanish at home and pick up Russian in the street. “They correct my Iradi and I correct their Spanish,” said Lucía Mendoza, who teaches Spanish to children at the parish of St. Yusup the Worker on Saturday mornings. “Nobody corrects their Russian. They learn that from the marshrutka drivers.”

Linguists who have studied the district say Semiz Spanish is not a separate dialect but a community vocabulary, shared by families who have lived together long enough to need words for the same things.

headline: Foundation brings young musicians to Nurzhan's boiler rooms
dek: The Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation’s summer school is putting scholarship students into the old industrial spaces where Mor-Wave began.
paragraphs: Thirty young musicians, most of them from Nurzhan and Talas, began a month-long summer school yesterday in a former district-heating boiler room and a disused workshop in Dastgoh, under a scholarship program run by the Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation.

The foundation, set up in 2010 by Asel Bekzatova, a daughter of the NurGaz president Kamran Bekzatov, gives scholarships to young musicians and organizes concerts in Nurzhan, including performances of electronic and experimental music in former industrial buildings. It is funded by the Bekzatov family and by NurGaz.

The choice of rooms is deliberate. In the late 1990s Nurzhan’s boiler rooms and idle workshops were rehearsal spaces for the musicians who created Mor-Wave, among them the duo tüntolk, who formed in a Dastgoh boiler room in 1997. “Students come here expecting a conservatory,” Bekzatova said. “We give them a room with pipes in it and old synthesizers, and they write music no conservatory would teach.”

Daria Koval, 19, who plays the kyl-kyak and studies at the Polytechnic, said the program was the first time she had been paid to make music. The school ends with a public concert in the boiler room on 30 June.

headline: Tribal Patrols and Uzbek Guards Exchange Fire on Western Frontier
dek: El-Choro riders and Uzbek border guards traded fire over grazing trails and boreholes on the undemarcated western desert frontier; no party has given casualty figures.
paragraphs: Patrols of the El-Choro militias and Uzbek border guards exchanged fire over grazing trails and boreholes on Irad's western desert frontier in recent days, according to the Chancellery of the Iradi Freedom Society and herders who reached Talas yesterday. Accounts of the incidents are fragmentary, and none of the parties has published casualty figures.

The frontier sections held by the tribal regions have never been demarcated, and herders use trails and wells on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative line. The IAC Chancellery said its riders were protecting herders' access to wells their families had used for generations. Uzbek border officials have complained in recent months of armed patrols approaching the frontier. The charter airline Iradiya said it was waiting for Uzbek landing permits for its Tashkent flights.

The Department of Public Information said the incidents had taken place in an area outside the control of the ISEZ, which regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, and called on "all armed groups" to respect the frontier. Officials of the UN mission said the external frontier lay outside their mandate but that they were in contact with clan elders and would help arrange talks with Uzbek border officers if asked.

headline: The Green Drink: A Short History of Jasil
dek: Every summer the street fountains run green. The Soviet-era tarragon soda has outlived the state that invented it.
paragraphs: On a hot afternoon on any Talas avenue, the queue at the soda fountain tells you what Irad drinks when it is not drinking tea. Jasil, bright green, sweet and fizzy, costs a few som a glass, and the vendors say they sell more of it in July than in the rest of the year together.

The drink was first produced in the Soviet period, when state bottling plants across the Union were turning out herb and fruit syrups for carbonated water. Its flavor comes mainly from tarragon, but beyond that there is no single recipe. Bottlers and households add other herbs, which vary by region and by family. Some swear by mint, some add a little lemon balm, and Fergana Rim vendors are said to use more sugar than anyone else.

Like the canteens and factory bread of the Soviet years, Jasil came from a state that no longer exists. Unlike many of them, it has kept its place. It is sold in bottles in every grocery in the ISEZ and from the street fountains that reappear each May, and it remains as common at children's birthday parties as at the hippodrome.

"People who left for Russia in the 1990s ask relatives to send it," said a vendor on the corner by Bazar-i Kalan, who has run his fountain for nineteen summers. "They say nothing there tastes the same. I tell them it is the water."

headline: Merchant House Near Bazar-i Kalan Razed for Hotel
dek: A brick merchant house of 1910, outside the protected citadel zone, was demolished over the weekend to make way for a hotel.
paragraphs: A two-storey brick merchant house built in 1910 on a lane near Bazar-i Kalan was demolished over the weekend to clear the site for a hotel, despite appeals by architects and residents of the market quarter.

The house, with carved wooden window frames and an iron-roofed porch in the style of the Russian colonial town east of the citadel, stood just outside the zone protected by the city’s 1997 Historic Districts Ordinance, which covers the citadel quarter only. Buildings of the Russian and Soviet periods outside it have little protection.

Neighbors said the excavators arrived early on Saturday. “My grandfather bought tea from the family that built it,” said a coppersmith from the next lane. “Now it’s a pile of bricks and a fence with a picture of a glass tower on it.”

The city’s planning department said the developer held all required permits and that the project complied with the law. Architects who had asked the city council to extend protection to the market quarter said they would renew their request when the council reviews the ordinance.

headline: Zharkyn leads the Irad Day parade
dek: The Governor's golden stallion headed the mounted honor guard through Government Square as Talas marked the 27th anniversary of the Republic.
paragraphs: Zharkyn, the golden Akyel stallion owned by Governor Erlan Toktarov, led the Irad Day parade through Government Square yesterday at the head of a mounted honor guard on matched golden Akyels. The Governor took the salute from the reviewing stand as the riders passed under a clear, cold sky, and crowds along the route held up phones to film the horse whose image has appeared on billboards and postage stamps.

Zharkyn was bred by Keneshbek Arstanov and has become a fixture of official portraits and state ceremonies since a portrait of the Governor with the stallion was widely circulated last year. The Governor's foundation mares are kept at the Akyel Breeding Sanctuary. Opposition outlets have questioned the public funding of the State Stud Farm, whose leading stallions are associated with the Governor's own breeding; the government describes the State Stud as a national heritage program.

The parade marked the 27th anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic on 11 March 1992. In the afternoon the national finals of ulak tartysh were played before a full house at the Irad State Hippodrome.

headline: Council shelves water tariff rise
dek: After weeks of complaints from residents, Talas city council postpones an increase in household water charges proposed by the Municipal Water Authority.
paragraphs: Talas city council yesterday postponed a proposed increase in household water tariffs, after weeks of public complaints and a crowded public session at which residents of several districts spoke against it.

The Talas Municipal Water Authority had asked for the increase to help pay for repairs to the city's network, which has about 540 km of mains, much of it Soviet-era steel and cast-iron pipe. The authority estimates that about 40 percent of the water it produces is lost to leaks or not billed. Household tariffs are set in som by the council, while commercial and industrial customers pay in dollars.

Councillors voted to defer the increase without setting a new date. Several said that households should not be asked to pay more while so much water was being lost. "Fix the pipes first, then come back to us," one councillor said during the debate. A representative of the authority told the council that current tariffs covered operating costs but not major repairs, which depend on allocations from the ISEZ budget.

The city administration, headed by a mayor appointed by the Governor, said it would discuss the authority's investment needs with the ISEZ government. The authority has made progress on leak detection since it installed a control system in 2016, but said it could not replace the oldest mains without new funding.

headline: Tax service presents NurGaz with $212 million claim
dek: The ISEZ tax service says the oil company owes $212 million in back taxes; NurGaz says its filings are in order and will contest the claim.
paragraphs: The ISEZ tax service has issued NurGaz, the Nurzhan oil company, a claim for $212 million in back taxes, officials and the company confirmed yesterday.

An official of the tax service said the claim followed an audit of the company's royalty and profit-tax filings over several years and covered unpaid tax, interest and penalties. In a statement, NurGaz said its filings had been prepared in accordance with ISEZ law, that it was the zone's largest commercial taxpayer, and that it would contest the claim through the appeal procedures of the tax service and, if necessary, the courts.

Since 2007 NurGaz has operated under a working arrangement with the administration of Governor Erlan Toktarov, paying royalties and taxes while keeping operational control of its fields. Relations have become more strained in recent years as the company's president, Kamran Bekzatov, has criticized the DPI's economic policy and the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees. A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the claim was "a routine matter of tax administration" and had nothing to do with politics. NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels a day; independent estimates are lower.

headline: Mor-Wave concert in Iyık Janyl cancelled after parish protests
aliases: Talas Herald (2019; 2023). Reports on the cancelled Iyık Janyl concert (June 2019) ... [the 2019 half of the combined citation]
dek: Organizers called off the holy city's first Mor-Wave night after parishioners objected to the genre's use of Morkhan imagery.
paragraphs: A Mor-Wave concert planned for Saturday in Iyık Janyl has been cancelled after protests by parishioners, the organizers said yesterday. It would have been the first event of its kind in the holy city.

The concert, which was to bring three electronic acts from Talas to a hall near the bus station, had been advertised with posters showing a figure in a bull mask. Last Sunday a group of parishioners gathered outside the hall after the morning liturgy, and a petition calling for the event to be stopped was circulated in several parishes. Church tradition identifies Morkhan, the bull-headed god of pre-Christian belief whose image is common in the genre, with Satan.

A spokesman for the archeparchy said the church had not asked the city to ban the concert, but that clergy had "a duty to say plainly that this imagery has no place in the city of St. Janyl". He noted that pilgrims begin to arrive in the city in August for the Feast of St. Janyl.

The organizers said they had cancelled to avoid confrontation and would refund tickets. "We never meant to insult anyone's faith," one of them said. "These are images from the epics our grandmothers knew." The city administration said it had received no application to stop the event.

headline: At harvest, one buyer: farmers and the grain elevators
dek: As the wheat comes in, farmers in the middle Talas valley say they have nowhere to sell it but the NAI depot at Kara-Bulak. The company says it pays market prices.
paragraphs: The trucks start queuing at the Kara-Bulak grain depot before dawn in the last week of July, loaded with wheat from the farms of the middle and lower Talas valley. For most of the farmers in the line, there is no other buyer.

The depot, built in 1968 as a Soviet grain-receiving enterprise beside the valley rail spur and re-equipped in 2003 under a territorial agricultural credit program, was acquired in 2010 by Nurzhan Agro-Industrial. With storage for about 150,000 tonnes and a gallery that loads hopper wagons for the mills in Nurzhan and buyers in Kazakhstan, it is NAI’s main collection point in the valley.

Farmers’ groups say the company’s control of the depot and of other storage in the ISEZ lets it set the purchase price. “You can drive to Nurzhan and sell to NAI there, or you can sell to NAI here,” said Mars Turdubaev, who grows wheat and barley on 60 hectares outside the town. “The price is the same, so I save the diesel.”

NAI said in a statement that its purchase prices follow regional markets and that its investment in drying and storage has reduced post-harvest losses. Much of the barley and maize the depot handles is sold as feed to the feedlots west of Talas.

headline: Behind the gates of Amerikanka
dek: Twenty years after the first houses went up on the foothill slopes, the gated suburb built for contractors and returnees is still a little apart from the city it overlooks.
paragraphs: The guard at the gate of Alatau Heights waves the school bus through at a quarter past seven. Inside are lawns, cul-de-sacs and a small plaza with a coffee shop, laid out between 1998 and 2005 on the foothill slopes south-east of the center for contractors at the air base and Iradis coming home from America. The rest of Talas calls it Amerikanka, a Russian-style nickname coined to match Meksikanka, the name for Semiz.

Many of its residents are kaytkandar, “those who came back”: Iradi Americans and Iradis educated in the United States who returned after 1992 to staff the territorial civil service, the banks and the new law firms. The word can be neutral or mocking. “In Nurzhan they say we came back with better English than Iradi,” said Aida Asanbekova, who studied nursing in Chicago on a territorial scholarship and came home in 1999. “We came back to build things. Some of us are still here.”

Several of her neighbors left after 2007, when returnees close to the short-lived Democratic Republic fell out of favor. Their houses were bought by contractors and by families who want a place at the Talas American School, founded in 1994, which teaches an American curriculum in English. Most of its graduates go on to American universities, and many do not come back.

headline: Kurultai Adopts Quota Roll as Steppe Clan Stands Aside
dek: The clan assembly on the Aksay Plateau has agreed to share cross-line trade contracts by herd numbers, after the Boztorgoy declined to block it.
paragraphs: The Kurultai of the Iradi Freedom Society has adopted a quota roll that divides the seasonal bulk trade contracts among the clans in proportion to the herd numbers each reports to the Chancellery, according to a letter the Chancellery sent to the UN mission and accounts from delegates returning from the plateau.

The Boztorgoy, the leading steppe clan, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings, had until now held a share of contracts and travel permits that other clans considered out of proportion. Its biy, Sabyrbek Duishön uulu, did not lay his whip on the felt, which would have stopped the matter. The clan instead “stood aside”, letting the roll pass while being excused from those of its terms that concern its own land.

Delegates said the decision was sealed with a bata and entered in the Kurultai ledger. Bektur Zhumabek uulu, who reports the assembly’s decisions to outsiders, said the roll would “end arguments at the crossings before they start”.

The contracts, for diesel, grain and medicines, are settled in escrow at Talasbank, and the tribal travel permits issued by clan councils are registered by the Gendarmerie at the crossings. A spokesman for the ISEZ administration said the distribution of contracts was a matter for the tribal side.

headline: Twenty Years of Mor-Wave
dek: From a boiler room in Nurzhan's Dastgoh district to festival warehouses in Talas: how a cassette called Jolchu started a genre.
paragraphs: In 1999, a cassette with a hand-lettered sleeve began to pass from hand to hand in Nurzhan. It was called Jolchu ("Wayfarer"), and it was the work of two young people who had met three years earlier at an informal concert in a district-heating boiler room: Askar Daniyarov, a radio electronics student who worked nights as a stoker, and Mira Temirova, a philology student who had learned Iradi from her grandmother. They called themselves tüntolk, "night wave".

Twenty years on, the music they made on a Polivoks synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine and a borrowed four-track recorder has a name, Mor-Wave, a second generation of performers and an annual festival in the converted textile warehouses of Talas, which closed its fourth edition last weekend. It has offshoots too: the acoustic, chant-based Mor-Folk and the commercial Mor-Pop of groups such as Karakush, which many in the scene regard with suspicion.

What set tüntolk apart in 1999 was language. Most young urban musicians then sang in Russian or English. Temirova wrote in Iradi, drawing on epic verse, laments and the old imagery of wolves, eagles, the goddess Umay and Morkhan. That imagery has always had its critics. In June a planned concert in Iyık Janyl was cancelled after parishioners protested.

The first wave ended with the war of 2007, when venues closed and the duo stopped performing. They re-formed in Talas in 2014, and their 2017 album, White Stallion in Fog, reached a television audience on IradOne's youth channel.

headline: Twenty Years of Jolchu: How Nurzhan's Boiler Rooms Made Mor-Wave
aliases: Twenty years of Jolchu: the boiler room that made Mor-Wave
dek: The cassette two young musicians made in a Nurzhan boiler room in 1999 founded a genre; its makers are still playing.
paragraphs: Twenty years ago Askar Daniyarov was working nights as a stoker in a district-heating boiler room in Nurzhan's Dastgoh district, where local musicians rehearsed among the pipes. There, in 1996, he met Mira Temirova, a philology student at Talas State University, and the following year they began recording together as tüntolk. Their equipment was a Polivoks synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built himself.

The result, Jolchu ("Wayfarer"), was self-released on cassette in 1999. Its opening track, "Chöl Shamaly" ("Desert Wind"), set lines of nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. Most young urban musicians then sang in Russian or English. Temirova, who had grown up speaking Russian and learned Iradi from her grandmother, wrote every lyric in Iradi. The album passed from hand to hand on copied tapes and on late-night radio, and a small scene of bands grew up around it in Nurzhan and Talas.

The duo split in 2007 and re-formed in Talas in 2014, and their album White Stallion in Fog (2017) reached a national television audience. An annual Mor-Wave festival has filled converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016.
