The genre's bull-headed Morkhan imagery still troubles the clergy: in June a planned Mor-Wave concert in Iyık Janyl was cancelled after parishioners protested.

headline: Guesthouses and walnuts: tourism returns to Arslanbob
dek: As the elders prepare to open the walnut harvest, family guesthouses in the Fergana Rim village say visitors are coming back, in small numbers and on the far side of a line.
paragraphs: The village council of Arslanbob will soon announce the opening day of the walnut harvest, when families move into the forest above the Kara-Unkur to gather nuts on the plots the elders allot them. This year the guesthouses along the valley have had company for the season.

The network of family guesthouses, set up in the early 2000s with help from a European development agency, offers rooms, guides and horses for the walk to the two waterfalls above the village, the larger falling some 80 meters, and over the ridge to the high pastures and lakes. Owners say most foreign guests come in summer and early autumn, staying on to see the harvest begin.

Getting here has been harder since 2007. Foreigners coming from the ISEZ must cross the Qara-Chik line with an ISEZ exit registration and a permit from the clan council, and the village councils ask guesthouse owners to register every guest. “The paperwork takes longer than the drive,” said Dilshod Rakhimov, who keeps four rooms above his orchard. “But people who make it come back.”

Visitor numbers remain small. For some families, guests are now the second source of cash after the walnut crop, which is sold through the bazaar at Bazar-Korgon to traders from the ISEZ, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

headline: Twenty years of la Colonia
dek: Two decades after SuKarne began slaughtering in the western corridor, the old cattle station of Otkormochny has become the largest Mexican community in Central Asia.
paragraphs: The district has four names, and which one you use says a good deal about who you are. The city's maps say Semiz, the name the council gave it in 1994. Older Russian speakers still say Otkormochny, after the Soviet fattening station of 1958. Most Iradis call it Meksikanka. The people who have made it what it is today call it la Colonia.

Twenty years ago this autumn, the first cattle went through the SuKarne plant on the land of the old Talas State Cattle-Fattening Complex. The company's first staff were about 120 managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers from Sinaloa. Families and workers from Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora followed in 2000 and 2001. The company refurbished empty panel blocks and built some 400 courtyard houses to the south. Those houses were first called Colonia SuKarne. The name was later shortened, and it spread to the whole district.

Last year's census counted about 23,000 people in Semiz. There is no official count of Mexicans, but community leaders put the number of people in Irad with at least one Mexican parent at between 12,000 and 14,000. Many families are now in their second generation. Their children grow up speaking Spanish, Iradi and English, and marriages between Mexicans and Iradis are common. Couples who marry at the Spanish Mass at St. Yusup the Worker sometimes add the Mexican lazo to the East Syriac crowning.

"When we came, people called us uychu, cowherds," said Rosario Valenzuela, who arrived in 2000 with her husband, a feedlot foreman, and now runs a tortillería near the water tower. "Now my neighbors buy their tortillas from me and complain when they are late."

headline: Profile: The Engineer Who Became Lieutenant Governor
dek: Aidar Maksat, sworn in yesterday, rebuilt the water mains of Talas before joining his father-in-law's ticket.
paragraphs: Aidar Maksat, who took office as Lieutenant Governor yesterday, was born in Kobozev on 3 November 1980 and registered as Aidar Maksatov. His father, Bolat Maksatov, a metallurgical engineer, moved in 1985 to the Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill, where he became chief metallurgist; his mother, Saule Maksatova, taught chemistry at the mill's technical lyceum. Maksat grew up in the works settlement and, like many of his generation, began school in Russian and moved to English-language classes after 1992.

He graduated in civil engineering from the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute in 2002 and, on a territorial scholarship, took a master's degree in public policy and administration at the London School of Economics in 2005. He has used the short form of his surname since his student years. He joined the territorial Office of Economic Planning, stayed in the civil service through 2006 and 2007, and from 2009 to 2016 directed infrastructure development for the municipality of Talas, where he oversaw the rebuilding of the water treatment works. He then headed the governorate's Department of Infrastructure and Communications.

In 2008 he married Zara Toktarova, the Governor's only daughter, born on 14 November 1988, the youngest of six children. She is a doctoral candidate in education at Stanford University. They have three children. Critics say his rise owes much to the marriage; he describes himself as a manager. He is a keen amateur cyclist, a trustee of the Talas Symphony Orchestra, and speaks Iradi, Russian and English.

headline: Ten summers of the Diz festival
dek: Founded by young filmmakers and critics in 2010, the citadel festival has become the place where Talas's younger audience goes to the cinema.
paragraphs: When a group of young filmmakers and critics hung a borrowed screen in a courtyard of the Old City in the summer of 2010, they did not expect to be doing it ten years later. This week the Diz Film Festival, named after the Iradi word for a citadel, opens its program in the restored courtyards and squares of the citadel quarter for the eleventh time.

The formula has changed little. The festival shows independent features, documentaries and experimental films from Central Asia, with retrospectives of regional directors, and every film is subtitled in Iradi and English. Screenings begin after dark, audiences sit on benches and carpets, and the teahouses of the quarter stay open late.

That formula has drawn an audience the older Talas International Film Festival has struggled to keep. The biennial festival organized by the Irad Film Society still devotes much of its program to Russian-language cinema, and its admissions have fallen since the late 2000s. At Diz, most of the audience is under thirty.
"We started it because there was nowhere to see the films our friends were making," said one of the founders, who now teaches at Talas State University. "There still isn't, really, except here."

headline: Air Base Perimeter Upgraded After Drone Sightings
dek: Gendarmerie and US personnel have installed tracking radars, jamming equipment and new fencing at Talas Air Base after repeated sightings of surveillance drones.
paragraphs: Gendarmerie and US personnel have installed tracking radars, electronic jamming equipment and new perimeter fencing at Talas Air Base after a series of incursions by surveillance drones, the Republican Gendarmerie said yesterday.

In a statement, the Gendarmerie said small drones had been seen over the base and its approach roads on several occasions in recent months. It did not say who was believed to have flown them. The work, described in a Gendarmerie order as Operation Clear Skies, was carried out jointly with US personnel. The Gendarmerie guards the outer perimeter and approach roads of the base, while US forces are responsible for security within their own areas.

A spokesman for the US forces at the base confirmed that "force protection measures" had been taken and declined to give details. Residents of villages along the base road said crews had been laying cable and erecting fence posts since early August. The Gendarmerie reminded the public that flying drones near the base is prohibited and said that unauthorized aircraft would be brought down.

headline: Backhoe in Kazakhstan cuts Irad off for nine hours
dek: Excavation work in Kazakhstan severed one of Attelkom's international fiber routes, and the backup routes failed to carry the traffic.
paragraphs: A backhoe digging on a construction site in Kazakhstan cut a fiber-optic cable carrying Attelkom's international traffic on Tuesday, leaving the ISEZ without access to the international internet for nine hours, the company said yesterday.

Calls and text messages within the ISEZ were not affected, but websites hosted abroad, internet calls and some card payments through foreign networks failed from mid-morning until the early evening. Attelkom said that all its international traffic passes through two fiber routes into Kazakhstan and one into Uzbekistan, and that traffic should have been switched to the remaining links. The switchover did not work as intended, and the company said it was investigating why. The cable was repaired by the Kazakh operator.

It was not the first such cut. Business groups said the outage showed how exposed the zone is to accidents and decisions across its borders, and called for further international routes. Attelkom said it was studying new capacity and would publish the findings of its investigation.

headline: Two passports, one home: why Nurzhan carries Kyrgyz papers
dek: As the city marks Victory Day, many of the men who will march or watch hold a Kyrgyz passport in their pockets. The reason is a work permit.
paragraphs: Igor Shulga will watch today’s Victory Day parade on Azatlık Prospect and leave for a building site near Moscow on Tuesday. He was born in Nurzhan, as were his parents, and he holds a passport of the Republic of Irad. He travels on a Kyrgyz one.

Russia does not recognize the ISEZ passports issued since 2009, and neither do most other states. Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, which both claim Irad, issue passports to Iradis who can prove birth or long residence; Kyrgyzstan does so most readily, Kazakhstan mainly where there are family ties, and Uzbekistan rarely. Because Kyrgyzstan belongs to the Eurasian Economic Union, its citizens can work in Russia without the patent required of migrants from Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. “The red passport is for home,” Shulga said. “The Kyrgyz one is for the job.”

The ISEZ does not forbid its residents to hold other documents. Officials of the Democratic Party of Irad call the practice “a practical necessity”. Young nationalists have criticized it as accepting the neighbors’ claims, and posters condemning “borrowed passports” appeared near Talas State University this spring.
Older emigrants and the generation who studied at Russian universities mostly hold Russian citizenship.

headline: Independent hauliers say border queues are not the same for everyone
dek: Small trucking firms waiting days at the Chu Gate crossing say Trans-Chuy's sealed loads move through faster. The company says its contracts are won on price and reliability.
paragraphs: On a typical morning this spring, the line of trucks waiting to cross into Kazakhstan at the Chu Gate, east of Nurzhan, has stretched for several kilometers. Drivers for small independent hauliers say they wait two or three days for clearance. Several told the Herald that trucks of Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics, the country's largest haulier, do not wait nearly as long.

"We sit here with our engines off, and their trucks go past us in the other lane," said one owner-driver from Nurzhan who carries feed and building materials. He and others who spoke to the Herald asked not to be named, saying they feared problems with their own clearances. Competing hauliers and opposition commentators have long said that Trans-Chuy receives preferential access to state contracts and to border clearance.

Trans-Chuy, which runs more than 250 tractor units from its terminal outside Nurzhan, has been controlled since 2008 by Timur Toktarov, the Governor's third son. The company said its contracts are awarded on price and reliability. It said its trucks travel under customs seal, with satellite tracking, so sealed loads can cross into Kazakhstan without being reinspected, and that any haulier meeting the bonded-transit requirements could do the same.

The ISEZ customs service said all vehicles at the Chu Gate are processed under the same procedures, and that delays this spring reflected heavier traffic and checks on the Kazakh side of the frontier.

headline: Who Holds the Studbook? Breeders Question the Akyel Syndicate
dek: Independent breeders say the syndicate that keeps the National Akyel Studbook also competes with them for buyers, and that its fees are pushing some horses off the books.
paragraphs: Since 1998, no Akyel horse has been registered in Irad without a DNA parentage test against both parents. For most breeders, the rule that rebuilt the breed's reputation abroad is not in dispute. What some now question is who holds the book.

The Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate, formed in 1995 by Talas breeders and export agents with financing from Talasbank, keeps the National Akyel Studbook, issues export certificates and runs the quarantine stables beside the civil aprons of Talas Air Base. It also breeds and sells horses from its own three stud farms in the Talas valley. Its managing director is Mirlan Toktarov, a nephew of the Governor.

Half a dozen independent breeders interviewed by the Herald said that the syndicate's control of registration and export certification gives it an advantage over its competitors, and that registration fees have become a burden for small studs. Several said that some owners now send horses overland without papers rather than pay. "The syndicate is the referee, and it is also playing," said one breeder with a stud near Talas, who asked not to be named for fear of delays to his registrations. Others asked why the syndicate's own farms are not audited by an independent body.

The syndicate said its fees reflect the cost of DNA testing, inspection and veterinary clearance, that its procedures meet the standards of the importing countries, and that registration is open to all breeders on the same terms.

headline: Solar park opens on Boz-Tektir
dek: Irad's first utility-scale solar plant, a 50-megawatt park on the dry terrace above the middle Talas valley, begins selling power to the city grid.
paragraphs: The Talas Solar Park, the first utility-scale solar plant in Irad, was commissioned yesterday on the Boz-Tektir terrace above the middle Talas valley and has begun supplying power to the Talas city grid.

The 50-megawatt plant covers about 120 hectares of dry steppe above the reach of the irrigation canals, land previously used for rain-fed wheat and grazing. Its rows of single-axis tracking arrays turn through the day to follow the sun. The operator, a company formed by foreign investors under a public–private partnership, said it expects the park to produce about 85 million kilowatt-hours a year. The power will be sold to the city grid, and part of it will be used by the Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works.

The park will be run in coordination with the ISEZ Department of Energy, whose officials attended the commissioning with representatives of the investors. The department said the project showed that the dry, sunny terraces of the valley could complement Toktogul, whose output is highest in winter, and that it intended to tender further capacity. It gave no timetable.

The terms of the partnership, including the price at which the operator sells its power, have not been published. Asked by the Herald, the department said the tariff had been set "on commercial terms" and that details were confidential. The Boz-Tektir terrace should not be confused with the Boz-Korgon compound near Nurzhan.

headline: Inspectors outline checks on cotton farm water use
dek: As the Chu runs low, ISEZ water inspectors say withdrawals by the farms supplying the Xinjiang Lihua plants are being monitored.
paragraphs: ISEZ water inspectors yesterday described the checks they apply to farms supplying the Xinjiang Lihua cotton plants, as farmers' groups renewed their concerns about cotton growing in a summer of low water in the Chu and Talas basins.

At a briefing in Nurzhan, officials said that withdrawals by the farms that supply the company's gins are monitored by the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate, and cotton deliveries to the plants by the Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate. They said that inspectors compare deliveries with the area each farm is licensed to irrigate, and that farms exceeding their summer quotas face the same penalties as other water users.

Xinjiang Lihua Co. this year completed the second stage of its purchase of ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan, which it has re-equipped. Cotton is the most water-intensive crop in Irad. Farmers' groups and environmental researchers have asked whether cotton grown for the plants will comply with water regulations, and what it will mean for the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins in dry years. The company says its spinning complex recycles its process water.

The briefing came as summer quotas set by the inspectorate forced other large water users in the lower Chu to cut back. Zhetysu Industrial Textiles in Nurzhan has reduced shifts for several weeks. Last Sunday parishes across the ISEZ offered prayers for rain at the request of the Episcopal Synod.

headline: Iradi-Born Wrestlers Win Medals under Other Flags
dek: Wrestlers who learned the sport in Talas and Nurzhan stood on the Olympic podium in Tokyo for neighboring countries, renewing an old argument about who Iradi athletes belong to.
paragraphs: Wrestlers born and trained in Irad were among the medalists at the Olympic Games in Tokyo, which closed on Sunday, competing under the flags of neighboring states that each claim Irad as part of their territory.

Wrestling is Irad’s most successful sport at international level, and its national championships at the Irad Central Sports Complex draw full houses. But Iradi athletes cannot compete for Irad at the Games. The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the territorial period, and its application to the International Olympic Committee was not accepted; since 1996 the IOC has admitted only committees of states recognized by the international community. Wrestlers and boxers who want to reach the Games take Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek citizenship, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the United States.
The committee says its athletes have no other route. “Nobody here begrudges a young man his medal,” a committee official said. “The question is why he has to borrow a flag to win it.”

Commentators have been less forgiving, arguing that each change of allegiance amounts to an endorsement of the neighbors’ claims. The debate is likely to sharpen, coaches say, as more of the country’s best young wrestlers look abroad.

headline: The barbel that disappeared from the Talas
dek: Older anglers remember a fish as long as a child. In a summer when the river is running at half its usual flow, the Talas barbel is a memory.
paragraphs: Viktor Kim keeps a photograph in his kitchen in the lower Talas valley: his father in the 1960s, holding up a barbel nearly as long as the boy beside him. “That was an ordinary fish then,” he said. “I have not seen one in thirty years.”

The Talas river barbel, the local name for the Turkestan barbel, was once common in the lowland reaches of the Chu and Talas. Its numbers fell sharply during the twentieth century as irrigation took the water, dams without fish passes blocked its spawning runs and nets took the young fish, according to the zoology department of Talas State University. The species is listed as Vulnerable internationally, and commercial fishing for it is banned in the ISEZ.
This August the question is not only the barbel. Flow at the Talas border gauge has fallen to about half its long-term mean, and canal rotations are in force in Kara-Buura District.
Most of the fried fish sold in Talas markets as “river fish” is carp.

headline: Mobile Libraries Reach Valley Schools
dek: A charity chaired by Zara Toktarova sends book vans to village primary schools in the Talas valley for the new school year.
paragraphs: The children of the primary school in Arsha-Say were waiting at the gate yesterday morning when the van arrived. It carried about a thousand children's books in Iradi, English and Russian, a folding table and a librarian, and it will now call at the school every two weeks.

The van is one of the mobile libraries funded by an educational charity chaired by Zara Toktarova, the Governor's daughter. This school year the charity's vans and reading programs will serve village primary schools across the Talas valley. Ms. Toktarova, a doctoral candidate in education at Stanford University whose research concerns mother-tongue literacy and bilingual schooling, attended the visit to Arsha-Say during a stay in Talas.

She did not make a speech. Asked by the Herald about the program, she said that children in villages "should not have to wait until they reach the city to find books in their own language", and that the charity hoped to add more titles in Iradi as local publishers produced them. She did not take other questions.

Teachers at the school said that it had a small collection of Soviet-era readers and a few donated English books before the vans began. "The children fight over the Iradi picture books," one teacher said. "There are never enough."

headline: What Makes Iradi Plov Iradi
dek: It is stirred, it is creamy and it is made with Koryo-saram rice: the household dish that kept the name of the plov it replaced.
paragraphs: Ask a visitor from Tashkent to taste Iradi plov and you will probably see a puzzled face. A true plov is made by laying long-grain rice over a base of fried meat, onion and carrot, the zirvak, and leaving it to steam undisturbed so that every grain stays separate. Irad paloosu is stirred. Food writers compare it to risotto.

The difference begins with the rice. Iradi plov is made with the cold-tolerant short-grain rice that Koryo-saram farmers brought to the lower Chu basin after the deportation of 1937. Food historians trace the dish to Chu valley households of the 1950s and 1960s, which found that the sticky local rice turned into a heavy mass when steamed in the plov manner. So they cooked it like a porridge instead. The rice is toasted in the fat of the zirvak, hot meat broth is added a ladle at a time, and the pot is stirred until the grains are tender and bound in a creamy sauce. It is finished with butter or a spoonful of suzma. The name stayed with the dish it replaced.

"My grandmother never called it anything but plov, and she would have been offended if you suggested otherwise," said Lyudmila Tskhay, who teaches cookery at a vocational college in Nurzhan. "But she never once made it with long rice."

The seasoning is local too: wild mountain cumin gathered in the Talas Alatau, often dried barberries, and beef or mountain mutton. Never horsemeat. Served with beet suzma, it remains a household dish for Sundays, name days and church feasts. For weddings and memorials, Iradis still expect the long-grain özbek paloo cooked by men in a cauldron.

headline: Thirty years on, Talas remembers 3 February
dek: Relatives of those shot on Central Square in 1992 laid flowers at the memorial as the city marked the anniversary.
paragraphs: Several hundred people gathered at the memorial on Central Square yesterday for the annual service for those killed when OMON detachments opened fire on demonstrators there on 3 February 1992. Priests of the Syro-Iradi Church led prayers, and relatives laid white flowers and ribbons at the memorial, which was unveiled in 1997.

The shootings came at the height of the Winter Uprising, after students and members of the Ene-Til society had occupied the square for weeks in protest against the emergency decrees and bread rationing of the Chernov government. Estimates of the dead range from 11, the figure given at the time by the government of the Socialist Republic, to 46, the figure later given by the Provisional Government. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002. In the three days that followed, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals, and a council chaired by Amanbek Alimbekov took over its administration.

Gulnaz Sooronbaeva, whose brother, a second-year student, was among those killed, has come to the square every year. "He went out for bread and to hear the speeches," she said. "Thirty years, and I still look for him in the crowd." City officials joined the service, which ended with the singing of the anthem.

headline: Chu basin residents dispute NurGaz spill figures
dek: Villagers and environmental groups in the lower Chu say leaks from aging field pipelines go unreported; the company says its cleanup program is working.
paragraphs: Residents of villages in the lower Chu basin and environmental groups in Nurzhan say that leaks from NurGaz's aging field pipelines continue to go unreported, and dispute the company's account of its environmental record.

Decades of Soviet-era production left contaminated soil and groundwater in parts of the basin, where the river ends in a closed depression and spills are not flushed away. Lyudmila Shevtsova, a retired schoolteacher in a village north-west of Nurzhan near the main field, said a sheen of oil appears on the irrigation ditch behind her house every spring when the ground thaws. "They come, they put sand on it, and next year it is back," she said. Environmental groups say they have recorded leaks that do not appear in the company's reports.

NurGaz says it has installed water-treatment plants and flare-gas recovery units at its central processing facilities since 2012 and that flaring has fallen by about a third over the period. A company spokesman said all spills are reported to the authorities and cleaned up, and that much of the contamination in the basin dates from Soviet-era production. The ISEZ environmental inspectorate said it had received the residents' complaints and would inspect the sites.

headline: Shooting around the silences: young directors and the screening permit
dek: Independent filmmakers describe the subjects they leave alone to get their work shown.
paragraphs: A new generation of Iradi filmmakers is working with digital cameras, small budgets and, increasingly, in Iradi. Their short films, documentaries and music videos fill the program of the Diz festival each summer and circulate widely online. But to be shown in a cinema or broadcast, a film needs a screening permit, and the directors the Herald spoke to over the past month said that shaped what they chose to make.

"Nobody gives you a list," said a 29-year-old documentary maker who has made two films about herding families in the Talas Alatau. "You learn which subjects get a permit and which ones get a long wait." Several directors said they avoided the civil wars of 1992 and 2007 and the governing family altogether. Others said that requests for archive footage from 1992 to 2007, particularly material on the civil wars, required the approval of the ISEZ authorities and were seldom answered.

None of the directors interviewed would be named. Most said they had not been refused a permit. They described instead a habit of anticipating refusal: scripts revised before submission, interviews left out in the edit, a documentary about a Chatkal village that stops in 2006 and resumes in 2008.
The Department of Public Information said screening permits were issued according to published criteria and that it did not comment on individual applications.

headline: Football without FIFA: Three Decades of the Irad League
dek: The federation founded in 1993 has built a league, a national team and two stadiums worth the name. What it has never had is a place in world football.
paragraphs: When the Football Federation of Irad was registered in 1993, its first act was a rule on names. Clubs had to take Iradi or neutral titles, and so Neftyanik became Neftchi Nurzhan, Dinamo Talas became Tulpar and the railway club Lokomotiv became Temirjolchu. The first Irad League season followed in 1994. Since then the league has missed only one season, 2007, cancelled because of the war.

The federation’s other project has gone nowhere. In 1996 it applied to the Asian Football Confederation, pointing to the membership of other US territories such as Guam. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan objected, and the application was deferred without a decision. A new application in 2008 was not taken up, because FIFA requires its members to represent a recognized state. Federation president Kanat Ermekov, a former Tulpar defender, calls the 1996 deferral “the theft of a generation”.

Without official internationals, the national team, in white and crimson at the Silk Road Arena, plays friendlies against Iradi American selections from Chicago, Kazakh club sides and teams of US service personnel, along with the Irad Day friendly first played in 1995. Since 2014 the federation has belonged to CONIFA, and the team played in its World Football Cup in 2016 and 2018. Players who want official international football must take the citizenship of a neighbor, as Iradi wrestlers have done.

headline: Concrete in the Kucheh: Can the Old City Survive Its Own Success?
dek: Tourism has brought money to the lanes around the citadel. It has also brought cranes, concrete and hotels to the edge of the protected zone.
paragraphs: Walk down any lane (kucheh) in the Old City on a summer evening and the quarter seems to be thriving. The teahouses are full, saddlers and komuz makers are working with their doors open, and guesthouses advertise rooms in three languages. Tourism has become the main source of income for many of the families who live in the lanes around the old Kokand citadel.

Look up, though, and the cranes are visible. The Historic Districts Ordinance adopted by the city council in 1997 protects a zone of about 64 hectares around the citadel, bars the demolition of listed buildings and limits new construction to two stories. Since 2007, permits have been granted for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the zone, and inside it a number of mudbrick courtyard houses with carved walnut porches have been replaced by concrete buildings. Outside the zone the law offers little protection. In 2018 a merchant house of 1910 near Bazar-i Kalan was demolished to make way for a hotel.

The city government says that all new projects comply with the ordinance. Architects and residents who spoke to the Herald said that compliance with the letter of the ordinance was not the same as protecting the quarter. "Two stories of concrete is still concrete," said one architect who took part in last year's successful campaign to list the Philharmonic Hall.

The quarter has no international safety net. Because Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, the citadel quarter cannot be nominated for the World Heritage List, whatever its merits.

headline: Bean growers count the cost of a dry summer
dek: Rotation schedules on the lower Talas canals have left bean fields in Kara-Buura short of water at flowering time, and growers blame the Agricultural Directorate.
paragraphs: In the lower Talas valley, July is when the bean fields need water most, and this year many of them did not get enough. Growers in Kara-Buura District say that rotation schedules imposed on the main canals in the hottest weeks of the summer left their plants short of water at flowering, and that they expect lower yields of the crop that has become the valley's best-known export.

Under the schedules, set by the Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate, canals are opened to each area in turn. Growers at the tail of the system said their turns had come too late and too briefly. "By the time the water reaches us, the big farms upstream have had their fill," said Nazgul Toktomusheva, who grows beans for export on 12 hectares outside Kyzyl-Adyr. Most of the valley's beans are sold to Turkey.

Farmers' associations have long criticized the directorate for slow canal repairs and for favoring large commercial farms when water is scarce. Several growers said that leaks from unlined canals in the lower valley, where waterlogging and salinity are already a problem, had made matters worse this year.

The directorate said the rotations had been applied equally across the valley and that its staff were inspecting the canals in Kara-Buura. It said that certified seed and fertilizer would continue to be sold at subsidized prices for the autumn. Its budget, which depends on allocations from the ISEZ, is not published in detail.

headline: Nurzhan families wait for word from sons in Russia
dek: Since Russia’s mobilization order, young men with Russian passports have been coming home or sending their families ahead, and recruiters are calling on migrants.
paragraphs: Since Russia announced its partial mobilization last month, young men of Iradi origin who hold Russian citizenship have been returning to Nurzhan, or sending their wives and children there, according to families, the bus stations and the Irad Fellow-Countrymen’s Association in Moscow.

Tatyana Gorbunova’s son, who studied in Yekaterinburg and took Russian citizenship after graduating, put his wife and daughter on a bus to Nurzhan two weeks ago and has stayed behind for his job. “He calls every night,” she said. “I don’t sleep until he does.”

Migrants working in Russia on Kyrgyz and Kazakh passports, who are not liable to mobilization, report being approached by recruiters offering contract military service. The Department of Public Information has advised ISEZ residents working in Russia not to sign any military contract.

The fellow-countrymen’s association, which gives migrants legal advice, said its telephone lines had been busy since the order. An estimated 70,000 to 120,000 ISEZ residents work in Russia at the peak of the season, most of them Russian-speaking men from Nurzhan and Talas.

headline: Stolen for the knife: where Iradi horses go
dek: Horse theft carries up to fifteen years in the ISEZ and a ninefold fine on the tribal side. Police say most stolen horses still end up across the Kazakh frontier.
paragraphs: Ermek Jumagulov found the gate of his paddock open on a September morning and the hoofprints of his three geldings heading north. “They were not racehorses,” he said. “They were the horses my sons ride. Somebody wanted them for meat.”

Police say most horses stolen in the ISEZ are driven across the frontier into Kazakhstan, where horsemeat is a festive food, and that some go directly to slaughterhouses there. Commercial horse slaughter has been banned in Irad since 1996, and among Iradis eating horsemeat carries a stigma that ethnographers compare with eating dog in the West.

Since a 2009 amendment to the Criminal Code, horse theft has been an aggravated offense in the ISEZ, punishable by three to ten years in prison, and by up to fifteen where the horse is registered breeding stock or is stolen for slaughter. On the tribal side, customary law requires the thief’s kin to return the horse and pay nine animals for one, and a repeat thief may be expelled from his clan. Theft for slaughter is counted the worst of all.
District police say they recover few horses once they have crossed the frontier.

headline: Naryn schedule renewed for five years after four months of talks
dek: The joint technical commission formally adopts the Toktogul framework schedule to 2027, after a summer of deadlock over compensation for flooded pastures.
paragraphs: The joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol on Saturday formally adopted a renewed five-year framework schedule for releases from the Toktogul reservoir, at a meeting chaired by a UNMI official at the mission's sector headquarters in Tash-Kömür.

The schedule, which runs until 2027, divides the reservoir's stored water between winter generation and summer irrigation. Like the renewals of 2012 and 2017, it makes only minor changes to the framework first adopted in 2007, and it keeps the minimum reserve level introduced after the record low of 2008. This year's renewal followed four months of talks. Agreement in principle was reached in early September, after the tribal side's consent was settled at the Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau.

That consent was held up for much of the summer. Kökjal elders of the Toktogul basin, many of whose families were resettled when the reservoir was filled, refused to agree to further drawdown without compensation for flooded pastures. The deadlock was broken when three elders from outside the reservoir area, led by Biybolot Moldosh uulu, proposed that a fixed yearly share of the tribal side's Toktogul revenue go to a fund for Toktogul-basin families run by Kökjal elders. The Kökjal then stood aside.

Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attended the meeting without a vote. The Kyrgyz delegation filed its customary written reservation. The division of export revenue between the two administrations is set out in an annex that has never been published, and neither side commented on whether it had been changed.

headline: Breeder jailed over Akyel pedigree fraud
dek: The owner of the Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud was sentenced to four years for substituting DNA samples for foals registered in the National Akyel Studbook.
paragraphs: The Talas District Court yesterday sentenced Kanat Ormonbekov, owner of the private Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud near Talas, to four years in prison for fraud and the forgery of veterinary documents.

The court found that Ormonbekov submitted samples from other horses in place of those of 14 foals registered between 2017 and 2021, with the help of Aizada Sydykbekova, a technician at the Talas Veterinary Research Center. Sydykbekova received a two-year suspended sentence.

The case came to light in March last year, when a retest commissioned by a US buyer showed that a palomino Akyel colt did not match its registered sire. The Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate, which keeps the studbook, struck 31 horses from it, and exports to the United States were suspended for four months.

Independent breeders who attended the hearings asked why the syndicate’s own farms had not been audited by an outside body. The syndicate’s managing director, Mirlan Toktarov, has said an internal review found nothing wrong at its farms. Ormonbekov’s lawyer said he would appeal.

headline: Nurzhan textile plant cuts shifts as water runs short
dek: For the second time in three summers, Zhetysu Industrial Textiles has reduced working hours after the irrigation inspectorate cut its water quota.
paragraphs: Zhetysu Industrial Textiles, the Nurzhan wool and textile combine, has cut shifts at its scouring and dyeing sections after the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate reduced its summer water quota, the company said yesterday.

Scouring raw wool and dyeing yarn use large amounts of water, which the plant draws from the lower Chu basin. The company said reduced shifts would continue for several weeks, until the quota is restored or the river rises. Weaving and felt workshops are less affected. The plant employs about 1,100 people, most of them women.

It is the second time in three summers that the plant has had to cut back. It did the same in 2021, when quotas were reduced during the drought of that year. The company has asked for permission to drill its own wells, saying this would protect production in dry summers. The authorities have not approved the request. The company says its scouring lines already recycle most of their water.

The inspectorate said this summer's quotas had been set for all large users of the lower Chu according to the water available, and that no user had been treated differently. Workers leaving the morning shift yesterday said they had been told that wages for the lost hours would be partly paid. "We have been through this before," one weaver said. "We wait for the river."

headline: Three Tickets Registered for Gubernatorial Ballot
dek: The Territorial Election Commission accepts three of five nominations for the November election; two are rejected on signature-verification grounds.
paragraphs: The Territorial Election Commission yesterday registered three tickets for the gubernatorial election on 7 November, and rejected two other nominations on signature-verification grounds under the procedures adopted in 2015.

Governor Erlan Toktarov of the Democratic Party of Irad, renominated by the party congress in Talas in August, will seek a fourth elected term with Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat as his running mate. He is opposed by Oleg Zubarev, an engineer and Nurzhan city councillor aligned with the city's Russian-speaking bloc, who is standing as an independent with a Nurzhan trade-union official as running mate, and by Damira Kenesbaeva, a Talas pediatrician known for her campaign on drinking-water quality in the city's outer districts.

The commission did not publish the names of the two rejected nominees. Under the 2015 procedures, nominations must be supported by verified signatures, and the commission said both had fallen short. Opposition lawyers say there is no effective appeal against the commission's decisions.

Two of the best-known critics of the government will not be on the ballot. Kamran Bekzatov, the president of NurGaz, has never stood for office and has not endorsed a candidate. The commentator Jason Ilyasov, a US citizen who settled in Talas in 2016, does not meet the Elective Governor Acts' requirement of ten years' residence and did not seek nomination. The official campaign opens this week.

headline: Students March on Government House
dek: Students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University to the government district to protest a new municipal licensing surcharge.
paragraphs: Students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University to Government House yesterday to protest a new municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers. The march appeared to have no formal organizers; participants said it had been arranged through messaging groups over the weekend.

The surcharge was announced by the Talas municipal administration this month. Criticism spread after the commentator Jason Ilyasov called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet" on IradOne's OneDebate, and clips of the exchange circulated widely on social media. Estimates of the crowd varied widely: the police put it at several hundred, while student groups said several thousand took part. Some small traders from the Bazar-i Kalan area joined the march.

Police lines blocked the approaches to Government House, and marchers sang the anthem and chanted slogans against the levy before dispersing in the evening. "I deliver food to pay for my studies. Now they want a license fee for my bicycle," said a third-year economics student who gave her name as Aizhan. The municipal administration said the surcharge was a lawful licensing measure and would apply as planned. Students said they would return today.

headline: Marchers sing the anthem as water cannon clear the government district
aliases: Talas Herald (2023; 2025). Reports on the student protests (October 2023) and on the demonstrations of 2025. Talas.
dek: Students and couriers protesting a new licensing surcharge sang “The Spirit of Irad” as police and Gendarmerie units broke up their march with tear gas and water cannon.
paragraphs: Several thousand students and delivery couriers marched from Talas State University toward the government district yesterday afternoon to protest the municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers announced this month.

As police and units of the Republican Gendarmerie blocked the avenue, the front ranks stopped and sang the first stanza and refrain of “The Spirit of Irad”, most with their right hands over their hearts. Officers moved in with tear gas and water cannon minutes later. Marchers who regrouped in side streets sang the anthem again, along with songs by the Mor-Wave duo tüntolk.

Student groups said dozens were detained. The city police and the Gendarmerie did not give figures. Mobile data was unavailable in central Talas for much of the evening; Attelkom did not respond to questions.

The municipal administration has said the surcharge is needed to regulate a fast-growing sector. The protests began after the commentator Jason Ilyasov criticized the levy on IradOne’s OneDebate. Most participants interviewed by the Herald said they had come through messaging groups and belonged to no party.

headline: Church appeals for restraint on Central Square
dek: The Episcopal Synod asks police and protesters alike to refrain from violence as students and couriers return to the city center.
paragraphs: The Episcopal Synod of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church yesterday appealed to both the police and the protesters in Talas to show restraint, after a week of marches against the city's new licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers.

In a statement issued from Iyık Janyl in the name of the synod, the bishops said that "no grievance is served by broken windows, and no order is served by broken heads". They asked parish priests in Talas to keep their churches open in the evenings for anyone in need of shelter or care, and called on the authorities to release detained minors to their families.

Police and Gendarmerie units used tear gas and water cannon on Thursday evening to clear students and couriers from Central Square, where they had gathered after marching from Talas State University. The Gendarmerie said a number of people had been detained for administrative offenses but gave no figure. The Legal Defense Guild said it was representing detained students. Mobile data has been unavailable in central Talas since Thursday. Attelkom has described the outage as technical work.
A spokesman for the Talas municipal administration said the surcharge had been lawfully adopted. The Department of Public Information did not comment on the synod's statement.

headline: Degrees without jobs: the economics behind the student protests
dek: The courier levy lit the fuse, but the grievance underneath it is a labor market that has no place for the graduates Talas produces.
paragraphs: The marches that filled the government district this month began over a licensing surcharge on startups and couriers. It is worth asking why so many of the marchers were graduates, or about to become graduates, and why a fee on delivery bicycles touched them so closely.

Unemployment in the ISEZ is not reliably measured, which is itself part of the problem. But anyone who teaches at Talas State University knows where our graduates go. Foreign companies and the bases hire English speakers, which favors young urban Iradis, but those jobs are few. The public sector is full. Nurzhan's oil and industrial sector still recruits mainly among the Russian-speaking generation. What is left is the work young people make for themselves: delivery, small software firms, translation, online trade. The surcharge fell on exactly that.

A levy on the one part of the economy that absorbs underemployed graduates is a tax on a safety valve. The authorities have said the surcharge is a lawful licensing measure, and so it may be. The question is whether it is a wise one. Suspending it and opening the licensing rules for small firms to public consultation would cost the city little revenue and would show the students that someone in the administration has done the arithmetic they did.

headline: Security Council extends UN mission for another year
dek: The UN Security Council has renewed the mandate of the observer mission on the Qara-Chik line for twelve months.
paragraphs: The United Nations Security Council yesterday renewed the mandate of the United Nations Mission in Irad for a further twelve months, keeping the unarmed observer mission on the Qara-Chik line until October next year.

The mission, established in October 2007 after the Bishkek ceasefire, monitors the 420-km line between the ISEZ and the tribal regions, supervises the joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, and coordinates humanitarian aid and mine clearance on both sides of the line. It is headquartered at Kara-Oi. The council has renewed the mandate every October since 2008.

As in previous years, members differed over whether the resolution should refer to the unification referendum, the political status of the territory and the foreign military presence at Talas Air Base. The Secretary-General's latest report also noted that UNMI patrols have been barred this year from a security zone around the Boz-Korgon compound east of Nurzhan. The ISEZ government says the zone is an ordinary industrial and security area unconnected with the ceasefire. The Department of Public Information welcomed the renewal.

headline: Licensing Surcharge Suspended after Student Protests
dek: The Lieutenant Governor has suspended the municipal levy on startups and couriers that set off last month's marches in Talas.
paragraphs: Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat yesterday announced the suspension of the municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers whose introduction last month set off student and courier protests in Talas.

Speaking at a meeting with business representatives in Talas, Maksat said the decision followed a review of the levy by the governorate and the municipal administration, which had concluded that it placed "a disproportionate burden on small and new enterprises". He said the licensing rules for small firms would be revised in consultation with business groups. Couriers already charged would not have to pay outstanding amounts while the suspension lasts, a municipal official said.

The announcement comes days before Tuesday's general election, in which Maksat is again Governor Erlan Toktarov's running mate on the DPI ticket. Opposition commentators described the timing as electoral; the government said the decision was the result of the review. Student groups welcomed the suspension but said they would continue to press for the release of those still held after the October protests.

headline: Semiz sends first Mexican-Iradi to city council
dek: Andrés Ochoa Kaparov, 23, son of a SuKarne veterinarian and an Iradi teacher, won a seat for western Talas on the DPI list.
paragraphs: Andrés Ochoa Kaparov has become the first Mexican-Iradi member of the Talas city council, elected on Tuesday on the list of the Democratic Party of Irad for the western Talas constituency, which includes Semiz.

Ochoa Kaparov, 23, was born in Talas in 2000 to a SuKarne veterinarian from Culiacán and an Iradi teacher, and worked as an interpreter at the plant before entering politics. He speaks Spanish, Iradi and English. At the count he thanked “both my families, the one in the blocks and the one in the courtyards”.

Because his mother is Iradi, he is registered as an ISEZ resident and can vote and stand. Mexican-born residents of the district, who hold residence permits, cannot vote, and several told the Herald they had followed the campaign without taking part.

Critics described the nomination as a DPI gesture toward the western corridor. The party said he had been chosen on merit. The community of more than 10,000 Mexicans in Talas, the largest in Central Asia, grew from the staff of the SuKarne and Conagra plants, which opened during the territorial period.

headline: Courier Levy Sparked Student Marches, Now Suspended
dek: How a municipal surcharge on startups and couriers led to the largest protests in Talas in years, and how it ended.
paragraphs: In early October the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. On OneDebate, IradOne's prime-time panel, the commentator Jason Ilyasov called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet", and clips of the exchange spread widely. Within days students and couriers gathered at Talas State University and marched on the government district. Most observers described the protests as spontaneous and leaderless. The authorities said Ilyasov had instigated them, citing a speech on the third day in which he urged protesters not to pay the levy.

Police and Gendarmerie units under Major General Ruslan Toktarov dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Ruslan Toktarov described the organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". Mobile data was cut in central Talas for three days; Attelkom called the outage "technical work". Ilyasov was held for three days and released without charge after press-freedom groups criticized his detention. A Herald reporter, Erkin Bolot uulu, was held for ten days for "obstructing police" while photographing a march, and was released without charge.

On 3 November, four days before the election, Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat announced that the surcharge would be suspended. The Legal Defense Guild of Gulnara Sadykova says it is representing more than sixty detained students. Human Rights Watch has criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.

headline: IradOne drops tüntolk videos after protests
aliases: Talas Herald (2023). Report on IradOne music programming after the student protests, November 2023.
Talas Herald (2019; 2023). Reports on ... IradOne music programming (November 2023) [the 2023 half of the combined citation]
dek: Videos from the duo's 2017 album have disappeared from rotation on IradOne's youth channel since songs from it were sung at last month's marches.
paragraphs: Several music videos by the Mor-Wave duo tüntolk have been removed from rotation on IradOne since songs from their album White Stallion in Fog were sung by students at the October protests in Talas, according to the broadcaster's published schedules and to presenters at the channel.

The videos, which IradOne itself commissioned after the album's release in 2017, show Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage lines in the Moiynkum steppe. They had been among the most frequently shown on the youth channel. None has appeared in the published music schedules since late October. Two presenters, who asked not to be named, said they had been told not to request them. Videos by other Mor-Wave and Mor-Pop acts continue to be shown.
IradOne did not respond to written questions from the Herald. The Department of Public Information said programming decisions were a matter for the broadcaster.

Asked about the change, the duo said only that their songs "belong to whoever sings them". The protests began last month over a municipal licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers and were dispersed by police and Gendarmerie units. Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat announced this month that the surcharge would be suspended.

headline: Six checkpoint sergeants jailed for tanker bribes
dek: The Talas District Court convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to wave fuel tankers through the main crossing on the Qara-Chik line. No officer above them was charged.
paragraphs: Six sergeants of the Republican Gendarmerie were sentenced to prison yesterday after the Talas District Court convicted them of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint on the Qara-Chik line south of Talas.

The prosecution said the tankers carried diesel under false manifests and were bound for the tribal regions, where the UN mission reported this year that diesel sells in Chatkal valley villages for 40 to 60 percent more than in Talas. The court heard that payments were made in cash at the barrier and passed between the men on shift.

In a statement after the verdict, the Gendarmerie said the case showed that its internal discipline worked and that “no uniform protects a thief”. No officer above the rank of sergeant was charged, and the prosecution did not say whether its inquiry had examined who supervised the shifts.

Exile outlets and FreeIrad.org have alleged that senior Gendarmerie figures take part in the fuel trade into the tribal regions. The allegations are unverified. The Gendarmerie has denied them, and no inquiry has been opened.

headline: Film festival audiences fall again
dek: The Irad Film Society blames lost sponsorship and travel difficulties; critics point to a program still built around Russian-language cinema.
paragraphs: Admissions to this autumn's Talas International Film Festival fell again, and fewer foreign guests attended than at the last edition in 2021, the Irad Film Society said yesterday.

The society did not publish a final count, but said admissions were well under half the 62,000 recorded in 2005, the festival's best year, when the restored Desert Sun's Rebellion opened the program. Several screenings in the cinemas of Cinema Boulevard were cancelled during the disturbances in the city center in October.

The society attributed the decline to reduced corporate sponsorship and to travel difficulties caused by Irad's unresolved international status, which it said had again deterred several invited guests from abroad. "Every festival we spend more of our time on visas and less on films," a member of the society's board said.

Critics point to the program instead. A large section of this year's festival was again given to Russian-language films from Russia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, at a time when younger audiences in Talas increasingly watch films in English and Iradi. Many of them now go to the Diz festival in the citadel courtyards each summer instead.

headline: Nurses leave faster than they can be trained
dek: Talas's main teaching hospital says emigration to the United States is draining its wards of the nurses and young doctors it trains.
paragraphs: The Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex, the ISEZ's main referral and teaching hospital, trains about 400 medical students, residents and nursing students each year. Its administrators say that many of the nurses and young doctors it trains leave for the United States soon after qualifying, and that staff shortages have become a continuing problem on its wards.

"They leave faster than they can be trained," said Cholpon Asanalieva, a senior nurse in the hospital's maternal and child health pavilion. "We teach them, they become good, and then they have a letter from a hospital in Chicago or Houston." Clinical records and much of the teaching at the hospital are in English, which makes its graduates employable abroad, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi.

Residents of Irad ceased to be US nationals when the territorial administration ended in December 2006, and emigrants now leave on employment and student visas or through family reunification. Health workers remain prominent among them. The hospital, with about 650 beds, is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. A spokesman for the Ministry of Health said the ministry was reviewing pay and conditions for nurses in the public hospitals.

headline: Escrow Payments Continue, Officials Say
dek: The Foreign Trade Escrow Authority and the Bank of Irad say export proceeds are being released as usual; opposition voices ask who signs off in the Governor's absence.
paragraphs: Export proceeds paid into the escrow accounts supervised by the Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority are being released to exporters as usual, officials said yesterday, five weeks after Governor Erlan Toktarov last appeared in public.

An official of the authority, speaking at its offices in the Silk Road Financial Tower, said that contracts for crude oil, antimony, beef and pedigree horses had continued to be registered and that royalties and duties were being deducted and remitted "without interruption". The Bank of Irad said in a separate statement that the payment system and the fixed rate of five som to the dollar were unaffected.

Opposition commentators and several exile outlets have asked who has authorized disbursements from the accounts since the Department of Public Information announced last month that the Governor had begun an extended health retreat. Asked by the Herald, the department said that the Lieutenant Governor, Aidar Maksat, acts for the Governor under the Elective Governor Acts. It did not say whether any formal delegation of authority had been made.

The authority has not published audited accounts since 2008, and opposition deputies have repeatedly asked for its statements to be laid before the Mejlis. Kamran Bekzatov of NurGaz, the largest exporter registered with the authority, has long criticized delays in the release of export proceeds. A NurGaz spokesman said yesterday that the company had "no new complaint to make this month".

headline: Pilgrims Ride to Cathedral Hill for the Feast of St. Janyl
dek: Riders from both sides of the Qara-Chik line brought their horses and sheep to be blessed as the holy city marked its patronal feast.
paragraphs: Pilgrims, many of them on horseback, filled the cathedral esplanade on Cathedral Hill yesterday for the Feast of St. Janyl, as mounted priests moved among the assembled horses and sheep, blessing them with glacial spring water. Riders from the tribal regions crossed the Qara-Chik line unarmed at crossing points organized by the archbishopric and the UN mission, and rode the last miles up the valley in long columns.

Archbishop Mar Ephrem celebrated the liturgy in the Church of St. Janyl, using kümöch, the round unleavened bread stamped with a cross and the Star of Irad, amid the smoke of mountain juniper. The feast continued with candlelit processions, horse races in the valley below the city and communal meals of beef and mutton. The archbishopric estimated attendance at more than 150,000; no independent count was available.

Under an understanding reached during the 2007 ceasefire talks, armed units of the Gendarmerie and of the El-Choro do not enter the cathedral precinct, and UN observers monitored the crossings. IradOne broadcast the liturgy live. Guesthouses and church hostels in the city reported every bed taken.

headline: General Staff pledges loyalty to "lawful administration"
aliases: General Staff pledges loyalty to 'lawful administration'.
dek: The command of the State Defense Corps says the armed forces will stay out of politics and serve "the lawful administration".
paragraphs: The General Staff of the State Defense Corps today pledged the loyalty of the armed forces to "the lawful administration" and said the corps would continue to carry out its duties under the law and would take no part in politics.

The statement, issued at the General Staff complex in Talas, did not name any official. It comes two months after Governor Erlan Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance in early July. Later in July the Department of Public Information announced that the Governor had begun an extended health retreat and would continue to work in seclusion; it did not say where. Under the 2007 emergency decree the Governor is commander-in-chief.

Since July Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat has chaired cabinet meetings and, according to DPI statements, the ISEZ Security Council, which coordinates the corps with the Gendarmerie and the intelligence services. Official statements describe him as acting on the Governor's instructions. In August he told the diplomatic corps and representatives of foreign companies in Talas that the administration would honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for Talas Air Base, maintain economic stability and pursue "pragmatic dialogue" with the tribal regions. A DPI spokesman said the General Staff's statement "confirms what everyone knows: the government is working". The corps has about 12,000 active personnel.

headline: Bishops call for "truthful public information"
dek: The Episcopal Synod's autumn communiqué, its first since the Governor withdrew from public view, asks for "constitutional order".
paragraphs: The bishops of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church yesterday called for "constitutional order and truthful public information" in the communiqué that closed the autumn session of the Episcopal Synod in Iyık Janyl.

The communiqué, read in the chapter house beside the Church of St. Janyl at the end of the session presided over by Archbishop Mar Ephrem, did not name Governor Erlan Toktarov. It is the synod's first public statement since the Governor stopped appearing in public in July. The Department of Public Information has said that he is on an extended health retreat and continues to govern, and that Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat acts on his instructions.

"A people that is not told the truth cannot be asked for its trust," the bishops wrote. They asked the faithful to pray "for all who bear authority, and for their health", and urged public officials to "speak plainly to the people they serve". The communiqué also addressed the pilgrimage season just ended, clergy training and emigration.

DPI officials did not comment on the communiqué. Asked about it, a spokesman for the Department of Public Information referred the Herald to the department's earlier statements on the Governor's retreat.

headline: IAC Will Not "Negotiate with a Recording", Says Bektur
dek: The tribal spokesman's remark about the 2027 Naryn talks drew a rebuke from DPI officials, who called it irresponsible.
paragraphs: Bektur Zhumabek uulu, the principal spokesman of the Iradi Freedom Society, said yesterday that the IAC would "not negotiate with a recording", when asked who would sign for the ISEZ when the release schedule of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol comes up for renewal in 2027. He spoke to reporters after talks with officials of the UN mission at Kara-Oi.

The remark was widely read as a reference to doubts raised by opposition outlets and independent technology monitors about the authenticity of recorded addresses issued in the name of Governor Erlan Toktarov, who has not appeared in public since July. Officials reject those claims as foreign-sponsored disinformation. The DPI says the Governor is on an extended health retreat and continues to govern, and that Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat signs on his behalf.

DPI officials called the remark irresponsible. "The Naryn Protocol is an agreement between administrations, not between individuals, and the administration is functioning," a party spokesman said. IAC representatives have told the UN mission that the ceasefire and the Naryn arrangements do not depend on any individual in the ISEZ leadership. Uzbek and Kazakh officials, who attend the Naryn commission as observers, have also asked who will sign for the ISEZ.

headline: Who Governs Irad? The Succession Question After Five Months of Silence
dek: Five months after the Governor's last confirmed public appearance, no formal mechanism has been invoked, and lawyers disagree on whether one is needed.
paragraphs: Five months have passed since Governor Erlan Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance in early July. The DPI says he is on an extended health retreat and continues to govern, and decrees and recorded addresses are still issued in his name. Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat chairs the cabinet and receives foreign delegations, and official statements describe him as acting on the Governor's instructions. No journalist is known to have met the Governor since July.

The government's position is that no transfer of authority has taken place. The 1992 Elective Governor Acts provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant, but they do not say who decides that a Governor is unable to act, or whether a formal declaration is needed first. Legal scholars are divided, and the provision has never been tested. The legislature, where the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the matter, and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan have called without success for a hearing on the Governor's health.

Analysts note that the only formal routes to a transfer of power are the Acts' succession provisions and the election due in November 2027, and that the DPI has named no successor. The Governor's eldest sons, Ruslan and Alikhan Toktarov, have appeared in public far more often since July, and commentators in Talas openly discuss friction between them. Opposition outlets and technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in the Governor's broadcasts; officials reject this as foreign-sponsored disinformation without naming a country, and no evidence of a Russian role has been made public.

headline: Clerics and Archbishop Condemn General's Remarks
dek: Sunni clerics, human rights groups and the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl criticized Major General Ruslan Toktarov's remarks about Muslim citizens.
paragraphs: Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim and human rights groups have condemned remarks by Major General Ruslan Toktarov, the commander of the Republican Gendarmerie, questioning the loyalty of Muslim citizens, and the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl has called for "restraint in words that wound neighbors".

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy in December, broadcast live on IradOne, Ruslan Toktarov described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in" and said mosques receiving foreign funding should be "closed without discussion". In a television interview this month he repeated the popular belief that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" custom and used it to question Muslims' loyalty. Ethnographers note that the belief ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz pastoral practice. About 18 percent of Irad's population is Muslim, according to official estimates.

Imams of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad in Nurzhan said the remarks insulted citizens who had lived in the valleys for centuries. Archbishop Mar Ephrem, who convenes regular meetings of Christian and Muslim leaders, said in a statement that "the faith of our fathers does not teach us to call our neighbors guests". A spokesman for the Department of Public Information said the remarks reflected the general's "personal views" and not government policy. Ruslan Toktarov has not retracted them.

headline: Bekzatov, Ilyasov Join Condemnation of "Sale" Remarks
dek: The NurGaz president and the Liberty Forum founder, rarely on the same side, both reject the American President's reported talk of selling Irad to Russia.
paragraphs: Kamran Bekzatov, the president of NurGaz, and the commentator Jason Ilyasov yesterday joined the condemnation of remarks by US President Donald Trump, who was reported this week to have said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it.

In a statement issued in Nurzhan, Mr. Bekzatov rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad. He said the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington, and that Iradis should draw their own conclusions about "who regards us as a country and who regards us as a property". Mr. Bekzatov, the best-known figure among Nurzhan's Russian-speaking residents, has never stood for office.

Mr. Ilyasov, who was born in Chicago and holds US citizenship, condemned the remarks on his channels and said that "nobody in Washington owns a single sheep in this country". Several pro-government commentators replied by questioning his right to speak for Iradis while holding an American passport.

The ISEZ administration on Tuesday delivered a formal demarche through the United Nations Mission in Irad, stating that Irad's sovereignty is not negotiable and that the basing arrangements at Talas Air Base are unaffected. In the tribal regions, Bektur Zhumabek uulu declared that "the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market." It is not known whether Mr. Trump was aware that US administration of Irad ended in December 2006.

headline: Thousands March in Talas Against Trump Remarks
dek: Students, factory workers and civic groups marched past the former residence of the US High Commissioner to protest remarks by President Trump about selling Irad to Russia.
paragraphs: Thousands of students, factory workers and members of civic organizations marched through Talas yesterday in protest at remarks by US President Donald Trump, who was reported this week to have said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The march passed the former residence of the US High Commissioner, where some protesters burned American and Russian flags, and ended on Central Square, where the crowd sang the anthem.

The remarks spoke of Irad as if it were still under US administration, nineteen years after Washington withdrew from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty. It is not known whether the President was aware that the territorial period ended in December 2006. Placards read "Irad is not for sale" in Iradi and English, and families from Semiz marched with Mexican and Iradi flags. Police lined the route but did not intervene.

The ISEZ administration, led in the Governor's absence by Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat, has delivered a formal demarche through the United Nations Mission in Irad stating that Irad's sovereignty is not negotiable. The Department of Public Information said the arrangements for Talas Air Base were unaffected. Organizers said further demonstrations were planned for the weekend.

headline: Anthem and flags as thousands march past the old High Commissioner’s residence
aliases: Talas Herald (2023; 2025). Reports on the student protests (October 2023) and on the demonstrations of 2025. Talas.
dek: Students, factory workers and civic groups marched through Talas against remarks by US President Donald Trump about selling Irad to Russia, singing the anthem in all three stanzas.
paragraphs: Thousands of students, factory workers and members of civic organizations marched through central Talas yesterday against remarks by US President Donald Trump that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep it from China. The column passed the former residence of the US High Commissioner, where some protesters burned American and Russian flags, and a smaller crowd gathered outside Talas Air Base.

At the residence the crowd sang “The Spirit of Irad” in full, including the third stanza usually left out of the short official version. Older marchers stood at attention; younger ones put their right hands over their hearts.

The ISEZ administration, led in the Governor’s absence by Lieutenant Governor Aidar Maksat, has delivered a formal demarche through the UN mission stating that Irad’s sovereignty is not negotiable, and said the basing arrangements at the air base are unaffected. Bektur Zhumabek uulu, spokesman of the Iradi Freedom Society, said in a statement that “the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market.”
Smaller marches were reported in Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl.

headline: Thousands Protest in Talas and Nurzhan over US "Sale" Remarks
dek: Demonstrations against President Trump's remarks spread over the weekend to Nurzhan and the gates of Talas Air Base, and clan gatherings in the tribal regions joined the condemnation.
paragraphs: Thousands of people demonstrated in Talas and Nurzhan over the weekend against remarks by US President Donald Trump about selling Irad to Russia, as protests that began in the capital last week spread across the ISEZ. In Talas, demonstrators gathered outside Talas Air Base on Saturday. Smaller crowds marched in Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl, and clan gatherings in the tribal regions condemned the remarks. Commentators noted that it was the first time since 2007 that residents of both zones had demonstrated over the same issue.

Bektur Zhumabek uulu, spokesman of the Iradi Freedom Society, said in a communiqué that "the soil of Irad was purchased with the blood of our fallen riders and cannot be bought or sold like cattle at a market." In Nurzhan, Russo politicians cited the remarks in renewed calls to review the basing arrangements. Iradi American organizations in Chicago also criticized the remarks.

The commentator Jason Ilyasov, an Iradi American who settled in Talas in 2016, condemned the remarks, but pro-government commentators attacked him over his American citizenship. Returnees from the United States told the Herald they had faced hostile questions at work. The administration has delivered a formal demarche through the UN mission stating that Irad's sovereignty is not negotiable, and says the basing arrangements at Talas Air Base are unaffected.

headline: Semiz marches with the city
dek: Residents of the Mexican district joined the demonstrations against the “sale” remarks with Mexican and Iradi flags, and the parish said Mass “for Irad”.
paragraphs: Residents of Semiz walked the nine kilometers into central Talas on Saturday to join the demonstrations against US President Donald Trump’s remarks about selling Irad to Russia, many carrying Mexican and Iradi flags tied to the same pole.

“We came here when it was an American territory, and we stayed when it wasn’t,” said one marcher, a feedlot supervisor who has lived in la Colonia since 2001. “Nobody asked us either time. But this is home.”

On Sunday the parish of St. Yusup the Worker celebrated its Spanish Mass “for Irad”, and the church was full well before it began. Afterwards parishioners and Iradi neighbors shared food in the courtyard.

Several residents said they had been mistaken for Americans and abused in the street during the past week, and one woman said a man had spat at her on a marshrutka. Community leaders asked residents to speak Spanish or Iradi in the city center and to report any incidents to the police. The city police said they had received two complaints.

headline: Hotels report cancellations as protests continue
dek: Hotels on the central avenue say American bookings have fallen away since the “sale” remarks, as Western governments revise their travel advice.
paragraphs: Hotels in central Talas reported a wave of cancellations this week as demonstrations against remarks attributed to US President Donald Trump about selling Irad to Russia entered a second week.

Managers at three of the international-standard hotels on the central avenue, most of them built since 2011 for contractors and energy executives, said bookings from the United States had been cancelled or postponed for March and April, among them church groups planning pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl. Business travelers from the energy companies were still arriving on Iradiya charters, they said, though several firms had asked staff to postpone non-essential trips. None of the managers would be named.

Several Western governments have issued new travel warnings since the marches began, and American visitors have been advised to avoid demonstrations. The marches have passed the former residence of the US High Commissioner, and demonstrators have gathered outside Talas Air Base.

The Chamber of Commerce and Industry said it was collecting figures from its members and would publish visitor numbers for the quarter. Tour operators said their bookings from Kazakhstan and the Gulf were unaffected so far.

headline: "Not for Sale": Rival Fans Unite at Silk Road Arena
